title: "Boxed only is flat" is not supported: its intervals contain the full fall
quote: On boxed answers alone rt is ﬂat (changes
explanation: Table 5 gives, for the two 5e-4 runs, an 'all' change of −2.6 [−5.3, 0.3] / −2.6 [−5.2, 0.1] and a 'boxed only' change of +0.7 [−2.9, 4.3] / +0.4 [−2.8, 3.4]. Both boxed-only intervals contain −2.6, so the data cannot distinguish 'boxed-only rt is flat and the fall is pure format share' from 'boxed-only rt fell as much as the total'. The point estimates also show that r_t(all) = r_t(boxed) x (boxed share among V'-accepted) is an arithmetic identity (e.g. 20.0% x 0.91 = 18.2 and 20.7% x 0.76 = 15.7), so the 'match' with the 91->76 and 93->78 shares is guaranteed by construction and is not evidence about mechanism. The prose treats a non-significant point estimate near zero as 'flat' while elsewhere (Sec. 3.4) insisting that null results be read through interval width. The conclusion that the fall 'matches' boxed share is an attribution by decomposition with no uncertainty on the share term.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Train-on-gold rise in r_t is mostly NOT a boxed-share effect, contradicting the stated explanation
quote: gives rt rises of 2.1–3.3 points as its outputs become more boxed, so
explanation: Using Table 5, the implied boxed share among V'-accepted is 18.2/20.0 = 0.91 -> 21.5/22.8 = 0.943 for Gold seed 1 and 18.0/19.4 = 0.928 -> 20.2/21.1 = 0.957 for seed 2. The share-driven part of the rise is about 0.20 x 0.033 = +0.7 and +0.6 points, while the boxed-only part is 0.943 x 2.8 = +2.6 and 0.957 x 1.7 = +1.6. So roughly 75-80% of the rise comes from r_t among boxed answers itself (+2.8 and +1.7), not from more answers being boxed. The prose conclusion 'rt moves with format for reasons unrelated to the verifier' is therefore only weakly supported; what moves is the fraction of correct boxed answers that sit on defect-affected problems (problem-mix composition), a third confound that the paper never names. This also undercuts the earlier reading that boxed-only r_t is the clean quantity (it drifts by +1.7 to +2.8 with no verifier in the loop, the same size as the self-training 'all' falls of −1.5 to −2.6 but of opposite sign), so the boxed-only 'flat' range of −0.4 to +0.7 is within the no-verifier noise.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: 'Adaptation would also produce' the boxed-share fall conflicts with the paper's own dose and control evidence
quote: to the defect would also produce.
explanation: The paper argues the r_t fall is explained by a falling boxed share and that adaptation would also produce this. But the defect fires on only 54-62 of 500 problems, and the pool holds 3-5 (5e-4) examples per round that avoid it. A 15-point fall in boxed share among correct answers over all problems (91->76) cannot plausibly be produced by adaptation driven by 3-5 training examples on about 11% of problems. The paper's own Sec. 4.6 hash control shows the boxed share falls 4.9 and 3.1 points on affected and unaffected problems alike with no learnable bias, and Sec. 4.4 says 'boxed share falls with the pool', i.e. general format drift (plus truncated training targets that lose their final answer, Sec. 3.4). So the more parsimonious reading is format drift unrelated to the verifier, and 'adaptation would also produce' is left as a logically possible but, by the paper's own dose argument, implausible alternative; the paper states both without reconciling them. Also at 10^-5, where the paper says outputs changed little (Sec. 4.2/4.3), Table 5 implies the boxed share still fell about 92% -> 86% (18.3/19.9 vs 16.8/19.5), which is not explained anywhere.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: "Pressure to adapt is therefore weak" is asserted from a count, and sits uneasily with the paper's own caveats
quote: pressure to adapt is therefore weak.
explanation: The inference is: only 2-12 pool examples per round come from affected problems and avoid the defect, hence weak pressure. (1) No dose-response is tested; the only varied-dose evidence (the \frac injected control, 263 vs 298 kept, i.e. 35 examples removed) is at a different learning rate and recipe and reports no count of avoidance examples. (2) The next sentences say the audit 'had little power to see any' adaptation and that without a control that shows an effect one cannot tell whether the audit would detect it; 'weak pressure' (a property of SFT) and 'weak audit' (a property of the measurement) are not separable with these data, yet the paper presents the former as a conclusion. (3) Rejection-sampling SFT is a positive-only policy-gradient step on a binary reward: on affected problems V removes almost all boxed correct samples (87-98%), so only unboxed completions survive as positives, which is exactly the selection pressure toward unboxing that RLVR has. (4) Check (iii) says the same defect changes about a fifth to a quarter of the pool (440->542), a large 'dose' by the paper's own standard, while the 2-12 count is a small one; the two counts measure different things (examples removed vs examples that teach avoidance) and the text does not say which governs pressure.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: RLVR contrast "a direct pressure that SFT lacks" is overclaimed and untested
quote: A false reject gives zero reward there, a direct pressure
explanation: In the paper's loop a false reject also gives the sample 'zero reward': it is excluded from the SFT pool, while an accepted sibling on the same problem is included. Filtered SFT (STaR/ReST-EM/RFT, cited in Sec. 2) is the standard on-policy, positive-only policy-gradient approximation, so the selection pressure is of the same kind as in RLVR but with fewer updates (fresh adapter each round, one epoch). The difference is of degree, not of kind, and the paper provides no measurement of either side (it says it has not run the audit on RLVR checkpoints). The sentence also reads as a mechanistic explanation for the null that the data do not provide, and conflicts with the paper's own admission that the audit cannot tell whether SFT adapts.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Injected-bias runs are labelled positive controls, but one cannot be and neither matches the audited conditions
quote: As positive controls for the audit we reran the loop once each
explanation: The hash-chosen 30% control is, by the paper's own statement, one that 'could not elicit selective avoidance' because a hash is not learnable from the problem; its expected outcome is null, so it is a negative control, and its null says nothing about audit sensitivity. The \frac control is a valid candidate positive control, but (a) it is run once, at seed 1, at 1e-4 with the corrected final-round recipe (k=2, two rounds), whereas the audit numbers come from 5e-4 and 1e-5 runs under the original recipe with the gold-storage defect, so it does not calibrate the audited measurement; (b) no count of examples in the pool that could teach avoidance is reported for it, although check (iii) and the Table 5 'Pool' column say this is the quantity that must be reported before a control is run; (c) no r_t or equivalent is reported, and the model also lost 7.0 pass@1 points, so training was damaging in that run. The Limitations section then counts these as 'two positive controls with no effect', which overstates what they are. The inference 'without a control that shows an effect we cannot tell whether the audit would detect adaptation' is correct, but it means these runs add essentially no information on sensitivity.

title: r_t is defined over a denominator that includes outcomes the audit cannot affect, and V' is not guaranteed to dominate V
quote: known defect class of the training veriﬁer V .
explanation: V' differs from V only on boxed predictions (it wraps the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains one). Hence every unboxed V'-accepted answer contributes zero to the numerator and 1 to the denominator, and r_t is by construction a product of a format share and a within-boxed rate. The paper says so, but then still proposes r_t(all) as check (i) and states that it is 'not a clean signal on its own', so the proposed audit's headline quantity is one the authors have shown to be confounded; the conditioned versions are only given post hoc and not as the definition. Further, r_t counts only 'accepted by V' but rejected by V'; cases where V accepts and V' rejects (possible when the wrapped gold changes parsing for a boxed prediction) are ignored, so 1 - r_t is not the fraction of V'-accepted answers that V also accepts unless V <= V' is verified; the paper does not state or test it. Finally the 'affected, parseable' subset is defined as problems 'where the defect ever fires and V can parse the gold', i.e. selected on the run's own outputs across all rounds; that is post-treatment selection, gives run-specific problem sets (24-28), and starts at 92-95% so near a ceiling, where changes can only be small and negative, and wide intervals (10-26 points) result.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Reading three same-sign falls as a pattern ignores non-independence and the opposite-sign controls
quote: We make no multiplicity correction, so we rest conclusions on patterns across
explanation: The audit conclusion rests on r_t falling in three runs (−2.6, −2.6, −1.5), each with an interval that contains zero or touches it (the 'all' intervals [−5.3, 0.3], [−5.2, 0.1], [−2.9, 0.0]); the paper calls this 'reaching or just touching zero' and the Abstract/Contributions report the fall of 1.5-2.6 as a result. The three runs are not independent replicates: all are generated on the same 500 problems, so the same 54-62 defect problems drive each r_t; two share a learning rate and recipe; and the third is a different regime (1e-5, k=8, five rounds). The pattern is also not uniform across the five runs in Table 5: the two Gold runs move +3.3 and +2.1, and the boxed-only and affected-parseable rows have mixed signs. With problem-level bootstrap intervals that all include zero, a 3-of-3 sign pattern can arise from shared problem composition. The paper explicitly applies this 'pattern' standard instead of a correction only in the audit and in the patch comparisons, while demanding strict interval standards for the main claims (Sec. 3.4), a mismatch of the self-consistency kind.

title: The audit is listed as a contribution while being declared non-novel and uninformative
quote: – A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect, carried over
explanation: Related work states 'Our per-round false-reject measurement (Section 5.3) is not new: it is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV', and Sec. 5.3 and the Conclusion say the result is uninformative about adaptation and that it needs a positive control the authors do not have. A contribution bullet whose content is (a) a method taken from prior work, (b) applied post hoc to one defect of the authors' own pipeline, and (c) shown to be uninformative leaves the contribution reduced to a measured storage defect and a cautionary note. Egashira et al. report that a policy first unlearns the behaviour that triggers format false negatives; the present data show a fall in r_t of that kind but interpret it as non-informative, without explaining why the analogous RLVR evidence was informative and this is not (the explanation would be the dose and boxed-share arguments, which are weaker than they look, see other comments). The title 'Mathematics or the Verifier?' and the Abstract's framing of a dichotomy are also at odds with the paper's own statements that the verifier branch 'cannot be settled' and the mathematics branch is a null for the recipe only (positive gate fails), so neither horn is answered.

title: Proposed items (iii) and (iv) are post hoc lessons, not audit checks, and (iv)'s notion of dose is underspecified
quote: (iv) Match training dose across designs. Our pooled design trained on about
explanation: Section 5.3 is titled 'A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier' but only (i) is an audit of verifier bias (and is shown uninformative); (ii) is a descriptive decomposition whose own text says the balance 'diﬀers by partition' (12-30% at seed 1, 52-72% at seed 2) and so is not a stable check; (iii) and (iv) are generic experimental-design reminders (count what a control changes; equalise training dose) learned from this paper's confounds, with no test that following them would have resolved anything. Calling them an audit protocol overstates; the paper does say 'not as tested methods', but the Conclusion then asserts what the audit 'must be conditioned on', which is likewise untested. On (iv): 'dose' is operationalised as examples per round (3,962 vs 872, ratio 4.54, checked), but update size depends on optimizer steps x learning rate. The paper states that Run A at 5e-4 uses about 195 steps per adapter; Design P at the default 1e-5 with about 3,962/2 = 1,981 steps gives roughly 0.020 in steps x LR against 195 x 5e-4 = 0.098 for the isolated run, so a dose-matched comparison on the paper's own grid might already exist and the isolated high-LR runs do decline (Sec. 4.4). This sits against the claim in 5.1 that the collapse 'does not reproduce under isolation'. Pooling adds a second dimension (two datasets in one adapter). Without a definition of dose, (iv) cannot be applied.
source_section: 5.3 A Proposed Audit for GVT with a Biased Verifier

title: Pool-count definition differs between the Table 5 caption, the prose and the Limitations
quote: only 2–12 examples per round from these problems that do so.
explanation: The prose says the pool holds examples that write the answers unboxed; the Table 5 caption defines Pool as 'examples per round from aﬀected problems that V accepts (and so avoid the defect)'; the Limitations call them 'training examples per round that could teach avoidance'. These are not the same set: V accepts a boxed answer on an affected problem in the 2-13% of cases where the defect does not reject (87-98% rejection where V parses the gold), so the V-accepted set includes boxed answers and is not 'unboxed'. It is also unclear whether the 3-5, 2-3 and 9-12 values are min-max over rounds or over subsets, and merging them into '2-12' mixes the 5e-4 and 1e-5 regimes. The 9-12 run (1e-5) has the largest pool but a 'weak' r_t movement (−0.2, [−4.9, 4.6]), while 5e-4 has 3-5; no run isolates a dose effect, so the range is not an informative summary. Since this count is the sole basis for 'weak pressure', its definition matters.

title: Section 5.2 'defensible statement' about the controls partly contradicts the dose caveats
quote: The defensible statement is narrow: removing a rare format defect, or the
explanation: Immediately before this sentence the paper says the data 'neither support nor rule out' the shrinking-pool explanation, that the patch tests a rare bias (0-4 examples; (iii) says this alone shows the control 'could not detect an eﬀect'), and that the no-filter control declines 'with more dose'. The narrow statement that removing the defect or the filter 'made no consistent diﬀerence at this resolution' is then presented as defensible although for the patch the resolution is, by the paper's own account, nil, and the no-filter comparison is dose-confounded. A statement about 'no difference' should be limited to 'we could not test'. Similarly, 5.1 describes the pooled decline as not reproducing under isolation while 4.4 reports that at 5e-4 every isolated run declines with sample-accuracy intervals excluding zero in all four A/B runs; the claim needs 'at the matched dose and rate' to be accurate.

title: Small numeric slippage between prose and Table 5, and shares quoted without a table
quote: On the 24–28 aﬀected problems where some form could, rt moves by −5.5,
explanation: Recomputing from the displayed Table 5 values: 87.2 − 92.8 = −5.6 (text/table −5.5), 92.0 − 92.3 = −0.3 (−0.2), 20.2 − 18.0 = +2.2 (+2.1), 94.7 − 95.5 = −0.8 (−0.7). These are most likely unrounded differences, but the table gives no note on this, and the prose range '2.1-3.3' therefore does not equal the difference of printed columns. Other checks pass: −2.6, −2.6, −1.5; +0.7, +0.4, −0.4; the 54-62 minus 29-34 gives 20-33 parseable problems, consistent with 24-28 only if the pairings differ by run; 3,962/872 = 4.5; 542 − 440 = 102 = +23%. The boxed shares '91->76% and 93->78%' are not given in any table and can only be checked indirectly (they reproduce r_t(all)/r_t(boxed) to within 0.1-0.3 points). The 24-28 and 54-62 ranges are not tabulated per run, so the reader cannot confirm that the per-run subsets in Table 5 match them.

title: Title and 'negative result' framing outrun a design that cannot see plausible gains
quote: The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the
explanation: The title ('No Detectable Gain'), the keyword 'negative result' and the Intro/Conclusion ('the ﬁrst answer is no gain that this design could detect') present the outcome as an answer to 'Mathematics or the Verifier?'. But by the paper's own numbers the design has a minimum detectable effect of about 10 pass@1 points (3.5-5.5 sample accuracy; 6 points only in the single-adapter ﬁnal round), larger than the 1-5 point per-iteration gains typically reported for ReST-EM-style self-training (the paper itself cites ReST-EM's 'diminishing gains after the ﬁrst round'). A null at 10-point resolution is close to uninformative about the effect sizes anyone would expect, and the MDE is a lower bound because seed variance is omitted. In addition, the point estimates are almost uniformly negative (in Table 2, 19 of 21 pass@1 changes are negative; only +0.7 and +0.0 are not), so 'no detectable gain' also understates what the data show. The body is candid about this, but the title, keywords and headline sentence frame an underpowered, post hoc, failed-gate experiment as evidence of absence; 'inconclusive' or 'no gain, and the recipe may hurt' would be the supportable framing.

title: Failed gate is the wrong positive control, yet the recipe is labelled 'corrected'
quote: The gate shows only that we have no recipe known to raise accuracy;
explanation: The abstract and Section 4.6 call the ﬁnal-round recipe 'corrected' and make the gate 'a positive gate that must raise accuracy for the recipe to count as able to help'. The gate is training on MATH reference solutions, and by the paper's own account it fails because the model adopts the reference style ($-spans 60 -> 1,577 of 1,600) and responses shorten by more than half (4.5), i.e. a style/length collapse that is speciﬁc to terse human solutions and cited work on self-distillation (Kim et al.). That does not show the pipeline is unable to register a gain from self-generated data, so it neither calibrates power for the loop nor justiﬁes saying the recipe is 'known' unable to help. Either the gate was badly chosen (a valid positive control would be an intervention expected to lift accuracy and independent of reference style, e.g. verified teacher or best-of-n data from a stronger model) or the recipe is not 'corrected'. The paper nevertheless leans on the gate to scope every conclusion ('the null concerns this recipe') while also using 'corrected recipe' in the abstract for the arm that shows the signiﬁcant decline. The gate was also run twice (rate rerun at 2e-5) while the loop was not rerun at 2e-5, and there is no check that a gate passing would have been the pre-speciﬁed criterion.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: The 'corrected-recipe' test is one adapter at one rate, not the multi-round loop the question asks about
quote: It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds; the loop has three
explanation: Section 3.3 deﬁnes 'ﬁve rounds' as round 0 plus four adapters and 'three rounds' as round 0 plus two adapters, so 'two rounds' means round 0 plus a single adapter (Table 4 indeed reports 'round 0 to round 1'). The ﬁnal round therefore tests one generate-verify-train step at one learning rate (10-4), yet the Introduction asks 'after several GVT rounds' and the abstract/5.1 say 'at any rate' and report the ﬁnal-round decline alongside the multi-round runs. The only evidence on the corrected recipe cannot speak to iteration or compounding (the paper's own restart-from-base caveat makes this worse), and the 'four learning rates' (and 'any learning rate') claims apply only to the earlier, self-described faulty recipe (512 cap with 43% cap-hit at round 0, 24-26% truncated pool, loss over the prompt, q/v-only LoRA). Aggregating both regimes into 'no gain at any rate' blurs that the recipe that was ﬁxed was tested at one rate and one iteration.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: 'Pooled decline does not reproduce under isolation' is contradicted by Run C and unsupported by the dose argument
quote: A sharp decline in a pooled design does not
explanation: The Introduction, 5.1 and the Conclusion state that the pooled collapse does not reproduce under isolation. But Section 4.1 says the pooled decline occurs 'on both datasets', and the isolated GSM8K run (Run C, 10-5) declines 12.7 pass@1 points [-21.3, -4.0] and 13.1 sample-accuracy points [-16.7, -9.8], an interval excluding zero, almost all in ﬁnished accuracy. So the decline does reproduce for GSM8K under isolation (smaller in magnitude), and at 5e-4 isolated Run C falls 22 points. Only the MATH-500 10-5 isolated runs fail to reproduce it. The replacement explanation ('about 4.5x more examples') compares Design P's pool to the MATH-500-only isolated pool (3,962 vs 872), although Design P trains one adapter on both datasets, so the relevant comparison is at least the GSM8K isolated run (about 2x Run A's steps). Moreover Design P (10-5 by default) has roughly 1,980 steps x 1e-5 versus about 195 steps x 5e-4 for the 5e-4 Run A, which declines far less (4-10 points vs 31), so a simple dose story is not even consistent with the paper's own runs. 5.3(iv) then converts this unresolved confound into a protocol rule ('cannot be attributed to pooling') while the Conclusion treats the non-reproduction as a ﬁnding.

title: Contribution '5.5-10.6 points' mixes in the no-ﬁlter control and the non-signiﬁcant run
quote: generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same
explanation: In Table 2 the 'Finished, matched' column at 5e-4 gives A1 -9.1, A2 -5.5, B1 -6.8, B2 -5.9, no-ﬁlter1 -10.6, no-ﬁlter2 -6.6. The upper end 10.6 therefore comes from the no-ﬁlter control (no veriﬁer in the loop), and the lower end 5.5 is A2 whose interval [-11.7, 0.1] includes zero. For the veriﬁer-ﬁltered runs (A/B) the range is 5.5-9.1. Presenting 5.5-10.6 as a contribution about the self-training loop at the highest rate attributes a control's decline to it, and shows that the 'ﬁnished-accuracy loss' is not tied to veriﬁer ﬁltering (the no-ﬁlter run loses the most; gold loses about 26). Section 4.5's 'ﬁve of six runs' also overstates independence: the six runs cover only two exam partitions (seeds 1 and 2), and the text names only the A/B pairs as near-replicates although the no-ﬁlter runs share the same partitions too.

title: Two incompatible 'bounds' (2.2 vs 3.5-5.5 sample-accuracy points) and an outcome-dependent 2.2
quote: ﬁgure of about 2.2 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a
explanation: I checked that 2.2 is derivable from Table 2: the largest sample-accuracy upper limits are +2.2 (10-4, seeds 1 and 3), then +1.3 and +1.0 (10-5). But the paper gives this alongside Section 3.4 and the Introduction, which say gains of up to 3.5-5.5 sample-accuracy points could have been missed (2.8h/1.96 from the same intervals). A reader can take the 2.2 as 'gains above 2.2 are excluded' and the 3.5-5.5 as 'gains up to 5.5 are not excluded' for the same data. The two ﬁgures are different objects (CI upper limit of one run's observed change, conditional on a negative point estimate, vs. a pre-data power threshold), and the 2.2 is the maximum over runs chosen after seeing them, for a measure chosen after seeing them, with seed variance omitted (the replicate pair differs by 3.2). It is repeated in 3.4, 5.1 and the Conclusion with a disclaimer each time, but never reconciled with 3.5-5.5, and it is missing from the Abstract and Introduction where only the larger ﬁgures appear. A single, consistently derived bound (e.g. pooled across seeds with a seed-level interval) would be cleaner; as written the post hoc 2.2 invites the reading the authors say it must not carry.

title: 'Patterns across runs' standard applied selectively; no multiplicity or sign-pattern treatment
quote: We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
explanation: Section 3.4 says 'we rest conclusions on patterns across runs and seeds, not on single intervals' and applies no multiplicity correction. Yet the treatment of the same pattern differs by section: at 10-5, with 4/4 MATH-500 pass@1 changes negative, 4/5 pass@8 negative and all sample-accuracy changes negative, it is 'a possible small decline, not an established one'; at 10-4 and 2e-4 no verdict is drawn although 5/5 sample-accuracy changes are negative; in 4.6 the pattern across three seeds becomes 'The loop does not help and probably costs a few points' (t-interval [-6.1, -2.1] with n=3); and the Abstract/Conclusion headline remains 'no gain'. Across Table 2 nearly every change is negative, which is evidence (a sign-test-like pattern) of a harmful recipe that the paper's own stated standard would support, but it is reported ad hoc where it helps the narrative. Conversely, the paper counts intervals excluding zero ('ﬁve of six', 'two intervals exclude zero') without noting that dozens of intervals are being scanned and that, per its own B-minus-A example (+5.3 vs -7.3 [-14.0, -0.7] from near-identical pools), the nominal intervals are anti-conservative for seed noise. The paper criticises others for exactly this kind of uncorrected single-run reading.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: The paper's own question (mathematics vs. verifier) is evaluated entirely with the training verifier
quote: by the veriﬁer (preset reward), the same veriﬁer that selects the training data.
explanation: The motivating sentence of the Abstract and Introduction is that a rising score 'does not show a model learned mathematics rather than what its veriﬁer accepts'. The paper then measures every accuracy (all of Tables 1-4 and the headline numbers) with that same verifier V (with a known storage defect that rejects about one in six V'-accepted solutions and 51 unparseable golds), and V' is merely a patched version of V. The paper itself notes that the PRM800K grader normalises \dfrac and \frac43 and 'could serve as a second veriﬁer; we did not run it', although generations are saved and re-scoring is cheap. Without any independent grader the design cannot separate 'mathematics' from 'verifier style', which is the question in the title; it can only report V-accepted rates. This is the same circularity the paper cites against RLVR gains, and the claim that the question's second branch 'stays open' is therefore partly self-inflicted rather than an intrinsic limitation. Most headline numbers before the ﬁnal round were also not re-scored with V' (only ﬁve runs were), so the 'no gain' claim for the other runs rests on the defective verifier; the 'ratio 0.73-0.85' is explicitly not used to adjust anything.
related_sections: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: The 'pre-set reading rule' has no operational thresholds and is applied with a post hoc 'detectably'
quote: requires pass@1 to rise, pass@k to stay ﬂat and style to converge
explanation: The rule is presented as pre-set and then discarded as one-sided. But it is never given an operational form (what counts as a 'rise' or as 'ﬂat', what margin, at which round, with which interval), and 5.1 evaluates it with a criterion the Introduction never stated: 'which never happens detectably (the largest rise is +0.7 [-6.7, +8.0])'. By point estimates alone, A seed 1 at 10-4 (pass@1 +0.7, pass@4 -0.7) satisﬁes the 'rise and ﬂat' pattern; the rule only fails once 'detectably' is added. 'Flat' pass@k also cannot be tested without an equivalence margin, which the design (8-10 point MDE) could not supply. The paper also says four measures were ﬁxed in advance, but 3.4 states that per-problem added/lost counts are exactly 150 x delta pass@k and 'not an independent test', so the pre-set list is really three measures. Finally 'pre-set' and 'ﬁxed in advance' are asserted without any time-stamped artefact (the code tag paper-2026-11 post-dates everything), while the status of every claim (pre-set vs post hoc) depends on it. The hindsight narrative is internally coherent (Intro, 5.1, 5.3, Conclusion all say the second branch is unanswerable), but the evidential weight of 'pre-set' is not auditable.

title: Injected-bias control: denominators conflated and shift in the opposite direction not discussed
quote: the gold contains \frac (70 of 500 problems; 263 examples kept instead of 298).
explanation: The same sentence mixes populations: '70 of 500 problems' (the full MATH-500 set, i.e. the exam) and '263 examples kept instead of 298' (from the 300-problem MATH-train selection pool). It is not stated how many selection problems contained \frac in the gold (about 35 examples dropped) nor on which problems the 95.0%/90.2%->87.4% boxed shares are measured (exam problems the model never trained on). The audit needs the share on the affected problems in the training pool to test avoidance. Also, the visible-rule diff is +2.8 against -3.7, -2.7 and -5.5 in unbiased seeds, i.e. relative to unbiased runs the affected problems keep boxing about 6-8 points more, which is the opposite of avoidance and is not commented on beyond 'no effect'. The biased run's pass@1 drop of 7.0 points is outside the 3.2-4.8 range of the unbiased seeds with a 12% smaller pool, and is not discussed either.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: 'Uninformative' audit vs. informative negative on adaptation: inconsistent reading of the injected-bias controls
quote: The model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised, but neither control
explanation: The Abstract says the two controls show no selective avoidance 'so the audit has no positive control and is uninformative about adaptation', and the Conclusion says the audit is 'uninformative about whether the model learns to avoid one veriﬁer defect'. But the visible-rule control is itself a direct test of adaptation under the most favourable conditions (every boxed answer on a learnable class rejected), and its outcome (no avoidance) is evidence about SFT adaptation, not merely about the audit's validity; 5.3 indeed concludes 'Under SFT the pressure to adapt is therefore weak' and 'We see none, in one defect class', while the Conclusion says the second question 'stays open'. The paper conﬂates 'the r_t statistic is unvalidated' (true: no r_t reported for the controls) with 'we have no evidence about adaptation' (not true: boxed-only r_t is flat at -0.4 to +0.7, and the controls show no avoidance). The text should separate these two claims; as is, the abstract understates the evidence for no adaptation and the discussion overstates the openness.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Audit's 'matches the \boxed share' claim lacks the available no-verifier negative control
quote: answers (91 →76% and 93 →78% at 5 × 10−4), a match that adaptation
explanation: I checked the arithmetic: r_t(all) = boxed-only r_t x boxed share among V'-accepted (20.0 x 0.91 = 18.2; 20.7 x 0.76 = 15.7; 19.4 x 0.93 = 18.0; 19.8 x 0.78 = 15.4), so 'matches' is exact and Table 5 is internally consistent. But the argument that the fall is format drift rather than adaptation needs a loop with no verifier pressure to show the same fall in r_t and in boxed share. The no-ﬁlter arm (Table 3, same seeds, with saved generations) is exactly that control, yet Table 5 reports only train-on-gold (where the model switches to reference style and r_t rises). The paper then states that 'boxed share falls with the pool, which both would produce' without giving the no-ﬁlter share. Using the arm it already has would test the claim directly and is the natural 'no pressure' comparison; omitting it leaves the central logic of the audit untested.

title: 'Four learning rates' is not a controlled sweep; abstract does not say so
quote: ams (150 problems; 500 in a ﬁnal round) at four learning rates on MATH-
explanation: The Abstract/Introduction/5.1 present 'no gain at any learning rate' as a sweep over four rates. Section 4.4 and the Limitations state that the 10-5 runs differ from the others in k (8 vs 4), rounds (5 vs 3), pool size and the pass@k metric, so 'only 10-4 to 5e-4 isolates the rate', and GSM8K has two single runs. Two of the four rates (2e-4 and 5e-4) have two seeds, and the ﬁnal-round recipe is at one further rate. The abstract's count thus overstates the amount of rate-variation evidence; the 8-10-point MDE for pass@k also mixes k=8 and k=4 rows of Table 2. This should be stated alongside the number in the Abstract.

title: Abstract's 'correct solutions' vs. rt deﬁned on V'-accepted; 'one in six' versus 18% at round 0
quote: the share of the loop’s own
explanation: The Abstract describes the audit quantity as 'the share of the loop's own correct solutions that a storage defect in our pipeline rejects (about one in six)'. r_t is deﬁned on solutions accepted by V', not on correct solutions, and the paper states it has no false-positive rate (the audit 'inspected only rejections'). Numerically, round-0 values in Table 5 are 18.0-18.3 (about one in 5.5) and 15.5-16.8 only at the last rounds (the quoted 15.5-18.3 range spans rounds), and the 440 -> 542 pool ratio implies 18.8% for the selection pool, not the 18.3% over all 500 problems; these are close but the single 'one in six' label hides that it ﬂuctuates by round and by subset, which matters because the paper's argument is about change over rounds of exactly this quantity.
related_sections: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Text and Table 2 disagree on B minus A at 10-5, and the 4.0 end of the '2.7-4.0' range depends on it
quote: seed 1 (recomputed from the saved generations; Table 2 lists values from the
explanation: Text: B minus A at round 4 is -0.7 at seed 0 and +0.0 at seed 1 (recomputed). Table 2 pass@1 values give B-A = -3.3 - (-2.7) = -0.6 at seed 0 and -4.0 - (-3.3) = -0.7 at seed 1. So the parenthetical about 'values from the run logs that diﬀer by one problem, giving -0.7' applies to seed 1 (a 0.7 shift), but the sentence is placed so that it reads as explaining seed 0. More importantly the Table 2 value B,1 = -4.0 is one of the values the paper says differs from its recomputation, and it sets the upper end of the headline '2.7-4.0 points lower' in 4.2. Using the recomputed numbers throughout (or showing both) would remove the inconsistency; the Table 2 caption acknowledges 'six round values' differ but does not identify which headline ranges depend on them.

title: Standards of rigour: forking paths, LLM review loop, tuning on the evaluation set and thin contamination discussion
quote: write the manuscript, the analysis and training scripts, and to run automated reviews.
explanation: The paper holds others to demanding standards (separate style from learning, control seed variance, report positive controls). It lists a long chain of post hoc changes (higher rates, controls, round count, primary metric, termination measures, re-scoring, the ﬁnal 500-problem round with a recipe redesigned after observing declines on subsets of the very MATH-500 problems later used as the full exam), and discloses that Claude helped with the analysis scripts and with 'automated reviews'. It does not say whether the automated reviews steered which experiments were added or which numbers were reported, which is a forking-paths issue the paper's own standard (Xu et al.'s seven measurement failures) would count. The six round values that differ by one problem between logs and recomputation indicate analysis-script inconsistencies. On contamination the paper gives only 'possible test-set contamination', although Qwen2.5-Instruct was ﬁne-tuned on MATH-style training data, the loop trains on problems from MATH-train and (in Design I) on 350 of the 500 benchmark problems themselves, and the gate is trained on reference solutions the model has probably seen; a self-training null on memorised problems is a different question. No analysis of these threats is given beyond the one phrase, and several single-seed claims (gate, bias controls, Run C) are made against the paper's own seed-variance standard.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: A null from a recipe the authors call broken is framed as a 'negative result' about verifier-filtered self-training
quote: the null belongs to this recipe, and
explanation: The title, keywords ('negative result') and the framing question ('Mathematics or the Verifier?') present the outcome as evidence about verifier-filtered self-training of a 1.5B model. The body then concedes that the recipe has (a) loss over the prompt, (b) a 512-token training limit that cuts the final answer and EOS from 24-26% of the pool, (c) LoRA on q/v only, (d) fp16 on a T4, (e) an untuned learning rate that was 'the default of our training code', (f) an instruction-tuned model that is restarted from base each round (little room to compound), and (g) a positive gate that fails by 32 points even after 'correction'. A negative result needs a method that is known to be able to succeed under the same measurement. Here the missing positive control means that 'no detectable gain' is equally predicted by 'self-training does not help' and 'this pipeline cannot help anything'; the data do not discriminate between them. The paper licenses only: 'for this specific pipeline, with a 150-problem (later 500) exam and single-draw pass@1, no gain larger than ~6-10 points was observed'. That is a statement about the pipeline and the exam's power, not about the model, the verifier or self-training. The caveats are honest, but they sit in Limitations and Discussion while the title, keywords and Abstract headline ('No Detectable Gain from Verifier-Filtered Self-Training') are the claim readers will take away; the mismatch is a framing overstatement. The research question 'is the model better at mathematics, or has it learned the verifier's style?' is explicitly left unanswered (Sec. 5.1 'The data cannot settle this'), so the paper has no answer to its own title question.

title: The main 10^-5 LoRA experiment is a null by construction (untuned, near-no-op adapter) and the defective components are never ablated
quote: is 10−5 unless stated otherwise; this value was the default of our training code
explanation: All Design I headline runs (A, B, C, k=8, five rounds, two seeds) use a LoRA learning rate of 1e-5 with batch size 2, ~200 steps and a zero-initialised B matrix. LoRA is normally trained at 1e-4 to 2e-4 (the paper's own final round uses 1e-4); at 1e-5 the adapter barely moves. The paper itself notes that length and cap-hit statistics 'barely change, which is weak evidence that the adapter did little' and that 'at 10^-5 the adapter changes the outputs little anyway'. A condition where the intervention did almost nothing and that yields 'no gain' is not evidence about self-training. The higher-rate runs then change k, rounds, pool size and metric simultaneously and use a recipe where 24-26% of kept examples are truncated before their final answer and EOS (so the model is trained to run on without terminating), loss is taken over the prompt, fp16 is used, and decoding uses top-p/top-k/repetition-penalty settings. The decline at 5e-4 ('less accurate on the solutions it finishes') is then exactly what such a recipe would produce independently of any verifier. The paper's mitigation for truncation (retraining without truncated examples) is reported only in the supplement and does not address the other defects. No single defect (prompt loss, q/v-only, fp16, lr, instruct vs base) is varied in isolation, so the reader cannot tell which defects drive the outcomes, and the final 'corrected recipe' changes loss, LoRA targets, cap, gold normalisation, data source and k together, so even its success or failure cannot be attributed.

title: A 32-point collapse from 300 reference solutions suggests a pipeline defect, so the gate does not show 'no recipe can help'
quote: isolate it. The gate shows only that we have no recipe known to raise accuracy;
explanation: The positive gate is used as the pivot of the whole paper (it converts the null into 'about the recipe'). But the observed gate behaviour is not that of a recipe that merely fails to help: one epoch (about 150 optimizer steps) on 300 MATH reference solutions drops Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 49.2% to 17.0% pass@1, and a 5x smaller learning rate (2e-5) gives essentially the same result (20.6%). A drop of this size that is insensitive to a 5x change of learning rate is much more consistent with an implementation or protocol fault (chat-template or EOS handling between training and generation, loss mask, adapter merged in fp16, response format mismatch such as $-delimited reference style the exam verifier handles poorly, or reference solutions that do not end with a \boxed answer) than with a property of SFT. The authors attribute it to 'the reference style but did not isolate it' - the simplest isolation (rewrite the reference solutions into the model's own boxed style, or train on oracle-filtered model samples with the same pipeline) was not run. Consequently the gate is not a valid positive control: it fails for a reason unrelated to whether verified self-generated data can help. This matters because the paper's central logical move is 'gate fails => null concerns the recipe'; if the gate itself is mis-specified, the same defect may also explain the loop's -4.1 decline and the loop's null, i.e., the pipeline is suspect, not just 'underpowered'. A correct gate (e.g., oracle-verified self-samples with V', or a known-good published SFT setup reproduced on this model) is needed before any recipe-level conclusion.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Pre-set primary measure (single-draw pass@1 on 150 problems) could not detect any plausible self-training gain, so a null is uninformative from the start
quote: The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the
explanation: The study fixed pass@1 and pass@k in advance, but pass@1 is defined as the correctness of the first of k samples (one Bernoulli draw per problem). With 150 problems this has a minimum detectable effect of about 10 points (and, per the paper, an underestimate because seed variance is omitted). Reported self-training gains for ReST-EM-type loops at this scale are a few points and are reported to diminish after round 1 (cited by the paper itself), so the design was powered only for effects larger than those that the literature suggests. Therefore even a pre-registered, perfectly executed pass@1 comparison would almost surely return 'no detectable gain'; the null carries little information about whether gains of 2-5 points exist. The switch to sample accuracy (lower MDE 3.5-5.5) was post hoc and still above plausible effect sizes. The 'about 2.2 points' sample-accuracy bound is explicitly 'not a power statement'. Moreover the Detectable-effects paragraph says 'a null here means no gain of at least that size', which misstates what 80% power means: at the MDE a real effect is still missed 20% of the time, and for smaller effects the design says nothing. The result should be reported as 'inconclusive below ~6-10 points', not as 'no detectable gain' in the title.

title: Self-consistency of standards: the 3-4 point declines are called real ('probably costs a few points') while the paper says its design cannot resolve effects below 6 points
quote: The loop does not help and probably costs a few points;
explanation: In Sec. 4.6 the loop's pass@1 changes (-4.8, -3.2, -4.2) are each below the stated 6-point detectable effect, two of three intervals touch zero, and the baseline itself moves by 2.4 points across seeds purely through sampling (round-0 pass@1 49.2, 46.8, 48.2). The paper holds that the corresponding positive changes 'could have been missed' and that intervals omit seed variance, and it dismisses the r_t fall of 1.5-2.6 points as 'uninformative' because intervals reach zero. Yet for the negative direction it adopts the opposite standard (the mean of three seeds with a t-interval of [-6.1, -2.1] and the abstract's 'falls 3.2-4.8 points in each of three seeds'). The three seeds also share the same 500 exam problems and (per Sec. 3.3) the training randomness is the only difference, so a t-interval with 2 degrees of freedom is fragile, and no multiplicity correction is applied across the many runs/measures. Symmetric treatment would say 'the decline is small, near or below the detectable effect, and may be sampling/training noise', or, if a -4 point decline is believed, then +4 point gains would be equally detectable with the same data. The text also places this decline next to a broken gate, so attributing it to the loop ('probably costs') is not licensed; the decline could be the same pipeline damage that produces the -32 point gate result.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Evaluation is scored by the verifier the paper shows to be defective, and the defect interacts with what the training changes
quote: through every run before the ﬁnal round, and every headline number is graded
explanation: Every accuracy before Sec. 4.6 is graded by the original verifier V, which the paper shows rejects 15.5-18.3% of the generations V' accepts, cannot parse 10.2% of the stored MATH-500 golds, and rejects \dfrac/\tfrac 100% of the time. The paper treats this as a constant offset that 'cancels in within-run differences only if those problems would not otherwise change, which we did not check'. It need not cancel: (i) the defect is concentrated on specific problems (54-62 problems, 94-98% rejection) so it is a fixed ceiling on 10-20% of the exam; (ii) training changes how often the model boxes answers, writes $-delimited spans or uses \dfrac, which directly changes whether the same correct answer is accepted by V; (iii) the kept training pool is itself missing those problems, so the loop never sees fractional/compound-answer problems and may drift specifically on them. The paper's re-scoring shows original-verifier changes are 0.73-0.85 of re-scored changes, i.e., headline numbers are systematically attenuated, yet all tables keep V and the authors decline to rescale. For the question 'did the model learn mathematics or the verifier?' the exam must not be scored by the very verifier at issue; the V' exam score (already computed for the audit) should be the primary metric, and the exam should exclude problems with unparseable golds. Also, the round-0 and later rounds are compared on the same prompts with a single temperature-0.8 draw for pass@1, so each comparison mixes true change with sampling noise that is of the same size as the effect (replicate pair differs by 3.2 points; round-0 differs by 2.4 across seeds).
related_sections: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Contamination of Qwen2.5 on MATH/GSM8K is dismissed in three words but directly affects whether self-training can show gains
quote: and possible test-set contamination
explanation: Qwen2.5 post-training data and pre-training corpora are known to contain large amounts of GSM8K/MATH-style data, and the 'first 500 GSM8K test problems' and MATH-500 (a subset of the MATH test split) are the public evaluation sets. The paper's final round also draws its training pool from the MATH training split, which Qwen2.5-Instruct was almost certainly trained on. If the base model already has memorised or heavily rehearsed solutions for these problems, (a) its pass@k on them is near a recall ceiling, leaving little headroom that self-training could elicit; (b) self-generated 'correct' solutions are largely regurgitation, so SFT on them adds no new capability and any perturbation of weights (an adapter at any LR) can only disturb recall, which is exactly the pattern of 'declines but no gains'; (c) selection and exam problems come from the same contaminated benchmark, so gains/declines on the exam are not measuring generalisation to unseen math. This undermines the interpretation of a null (and of the declines at higher rates) for 'does self-training improve mathematics'. A contamination-robust evaluation (post-cutoff problems, a perturbed/rephrased benchmark, or a non-leaked set) or at least a contamination probe (e.g., truncated-prompt completion, paraphrase sensitivity) is needed; the limitation is stated but not examined or bounded, and the conclusions are not conditioned on it.
related_sections: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Cross-run causal statements rest on runs with different optimizer-step budgets
quote: it took about twice Run A’s optimizer steps
explanation: The paper correctly flags that Run C used ~2x the optimizer steps of Run A, the no-filter control 3-4x, and the pooled design ~4.5x (also different datasets/adapters/eval-on-selection). But the subsequent text still draws directional conclusions from these comparisons: 'Removing the filter is not better than keeping it' and 'lower on pass@4 at both seeds'; 'the no-filter control declines without any veriﬁer' (Sec. 5.2); the 5e-4 decline 'may grow with the rate' (k, pool and rounds also change between rate groups); and 'the model is less accurate on the solutions it ﬁnishes' in the Conclusion. In SFT with a fixed LR, accuracy loss is largely a function of total update magnitude (LR x steps x data distribution shift), so a 3-4x dose difference is not a nuisance but the main driver, and the no-filter arm's truncation rate (62.4% vs 24.5%) is a second large confound. The paper offers no matched-dose arm (e.g., unfiltered or random-subset training with the same number of steps and the same pool size as Run A), so none of these comparisons can support even weak directional statements about the verifier's role. The treatment is also asymmetric: the B-A sign flip (+5.3 vs -7.3) is explained as 'trajectory noise', while other differences of comparable size across runs with unmatched dose are read as informative. Because these comparisons are the paper's only handle on the 'verifier' half of the title, the weakness is central, not peripheral.

title: The 'cap-share decomposition' is not a meaningful decomposition: unstable, conditioned on a post-treatment variable, and measuring an artefact of the recipe
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
explanation: The decomposition splits the sample-accuracy decline into a finished-accuracy part and a cap-share part. (1) The shares are not stable across partitions: 12-30% at seed 1, -2% and 5% in two further runs, 52-72% at seed 2, so the quantity changes with the exam partition more than with the treatment; with exam sets of 150 problems and intervals that mostly touch zero it cannot be distinguished from noise. (2) 'Finished' accuracy is measured on the subset of generations that end before the cap, i.e., conditioned on a post-treatment variable (which problems finish after training); the authors concede it 'conditions on which problems finish after training, so it is descriptive'. Selection into 'finished' (shorter, easier problems) changes with training, so the 'matched' comparison is not like-for-like and any attribution of percentages to parts is order- and weighting-dependent (interaction term). (3) 40-46% of round-0 generations already hit the 512 cap and the training set truncates 24-26% of examples before their final answer and EOS, so the cap-hit share is substantially a consequence of the paper's own recipe (teaching the model to run on) rather than a property of self-training; decomposing the decline along an artefact of the setup yields a number about the artefact. (4) Cap-hit is defined by re-tokenising decoded text at >=508 tokens because generation-time token counts 'were not saved', and the 1,536-token re-scoring that supports 'leaves the deficit in place' was also not saved. Elevating this to a recommended audit step (ii) ('Decompose declines under a fixed cap') overstates a descriptive, unstable, non-causal split; a proper alternative is to re-evaluate at a cap that rarely binds (a rerun), which the authors say they did not retain.

title: Generic decoding settings (repetition penalty 1.1, T=0.8) likely depress the baseline and inflate cap hits, confounding every round-to-round comparison
quote: temperature 0.8 with a cap of 512 new tokens
explanation: Generation uses temperature 0.8 with the checkpoint's default repetition penalty of 1.1 and a 512-token cap. A repetition penalty penalises re-use of digits, LaTeX tokens and variable names that are intrinsic to multi-step math, and is known to degrade or destabilise mathematical derivations; combined with sampling at 0.8, it produces long, rambling outputs (43% of round-0 generations hit the cap). So the 'untrained' baseline is itself a depressed, noisy operating point (49% MATH-500 for a model that is normally reported at higher accuracy under greedy decoding with a larger budget). Self-training that merely makes outputs shorter or more deterministic can then move accuracy for reasons unrelated to mathematics or verifier learning, and the adapter-trained model is also sampled with the same penalty over the training distribution that was itself generated under it. The paper does not report greedy/low-temperature accuracy, or a larger cap, as a reference, so the size of any gain that a fair baseline could leave room for is unknown, and the 'cap binds from the start' observation is an artefact that the study chose.

title: 'Drift' versus 'imitation' is never operationalised, and the observed declines are explained equally by generic SFT damage
quote: drift: boxed share falls with the pool, which both would produce.
explanation: The framing question contrasts 'learning mathematics' with 'learning what the verifier accepts', and Sec. 4.4 and 5.2 discuss 'imitation' and 'drift' as rival accounts of the declines. Neither term is given a testable definition or a measurable signature, and the paper then reports that its style measure does not separate them. Moreover, the boxed share falls 'with the pool', but the pool contracts because boxed (parseable) answers decline: the explanation is circular. The key alternative - generic parameter damage from SFT with high LR, prompt loss, q/v-only LoRA, fp16 and truncated examples - predicts the same declines, and is supported by the paper's own controls: the no-filter arm (no verifier) declines as much or more (-8 to -10 sample-accuracy points), and training on gold (no verifier) collapses by 20-32 points. These show that the decline is not specific to verifier selection at all. The Conclusion's wording ('the model is less accurate on the solutions it ﬁnishes') is thus a description of damage under this recipe, not evidence about verifier imitation or drift, and the Discussion's 'self-reinforcing shrinking pool shaped by the biased verifier' is acknowledged to be untested. The paper should drop the drift/imitation vocabulary from the headline or specify a pre-defined discriminating prediction (e.g., a V vs V' run where only V-induced style should differ).

title: Missing matched-dose unfiltered/random baseline and a V'-trained run mean the 'verifier' half of the contribution has no manipulation
quote: No run varies the frequent gold-storage defect, and the
explanation: The title asks about the verifier, but the only verifier manipulations are (a) a patch that changes 0-4 training examples (acknowledged to be undetectable by prevalence alone) and (b) removing the filter at 3-4x dose. The paper itself identifies the real manipulation - a repaired verifier V' that fixes a defect rejecting ~one in six correct generations and shifts the pool by +23% (440 -> 542) - and already has V' implemented (it is used for post hoc re-scoring and r_t). Yet no loop was trained with V' (the final round uses normalised gold answers, which silently removes the defect but changes six other things at once), no random-selection or unfiltered baseline at matched steps and matched pool size exists, and no injected-bias control produced any effect (so the audit has no positive control). Without these, the verifier-specific claims reduce to 'we looked at r_t and it moved with the boxed share'. The post hoc audit, framed as the contribution that distinguishes this paper from TinyV/Egashira et al., is acknowledged to have 'no positive control and is uninformative about adaptation'. The remaining contribution is a null result for an unvalidated pipeline plus a list of caveats. The experiment that would actually separate the explanations (V vs V' vs matched-dose random subset, same steps, same pipeline, exam scored by V') is cheap compared with the three-seed final round and should be run or the title/abstract should not promise to answer the verifier question.
related_sections: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: Reproducibility: key supporting outputs were not saved, and AI-written analysis scripts show unreconciled inconsistencies with run logs
quote: Design P’s training logs and the 1,536-token re-scoring outputs were not saved.
explanation: The Code availability statement admits that Design P's training logs, generation-time token counts and the 1,536-token re-scoring outputs were not saved. Yet claims in the body depend on them: the Design P 'collapse' headline (Sec. 4.1, 50.0 -> 18.6 pass@1) and the statement that 're-scoring at a 1,536-token cap leaves the deficit in place', and the cap-hit statistic is a proxy via re-tokenisation (>=508 tokens) rather than actual generation-time stopping. These claims therefore cannot be re-checked. The 'Use of AI tools' statement says Claude wrote the manuscript, the analysis scripts and the training scripts; combined with the paper's own admissions that 'six round values differ by one problem' between logs and recomputation, that Table 2 mixes log values with recomputed values (-0.7 vs recomputed), that multiple versions of the same quantity are in circulation (e.g., B, seed 1 round-4 pass@8 58.0% vs 58.7%), and that the audit script (rt_audit.py) was written after the fact for a defect found post hoc, an independent verification of the analysis code is warranted (a unit-tested recomputation from raw generations of every table, with the code version pinned by tag and hashes of the saved generations). The disclosure itself is adequate in that it names the tool and responsibility, but it does not specify which results were produced/verified by AI-written scripts versus by hand, nor how correctness of those scripts was validated, which is material given the reported discrepancies and the many post hoc analyses. Pinning a single tag (paper-2026-11) is helpful only if every reported number is reproducible at that tag from saved artefacts, which the unsaved logs preclude for part of the paper.

title: "Corrected recipe" label is contradicted by the failed gate; the correction was never validated
quote: Because no earlier arm improved, we ran one last round with the recipe changes that remove the suspected causes
explanation: The section title, abstract ("with a corrected recipe") and Sections 6-7 ("even with a corrected recipe") call the recipe corrected, but the only test of whether it can improve accuracy (the positive gate) fails by 32 points at both 1e-4 and 2e-5. The text then concedes "we have no recipe known to raise accuracy". A recipe that cannot raise accuracy on reference solutions has not been shown to have removed the causes of earlier failure; 'corrected' is an untested hypothesis stated as a result. In addition the suspected causes were identified post hoc after seeing the earlier null (Sec. 4.5 is explicitly post hoc), so the choice of changes is outcome-driven. The adjective should be dropped or the claim reframed as 'a modified recipe'.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Seven simultaneous recipe changes; no ablation, so neither the gate failure nor the loop decline can be attributed
quote:
loss on the completion only, LoRA on all
linear layers, a 1,024-token cap and training limit, normalised gold answers, and
a pool of 300 problems from the MATH training split, so that the exam is all 500
MATH-500 problems. It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds
explanation: Relative to Design I the final round changes loss masking, LoRA target modules, cap, gold normalisation, pool source and size, exam size, k and number of rounds together. Any difference from earlier results (e.g. pass@1 falling 3.2-4.8 with a 500-problem exam versus no detectable change with 150) is confounded with all of these, and the paper itself notes the earlier cap decomposition (Sec. 4.5) no longer applies at 1,024 tokens. All-linear LoRA at 1e-4 on only ~300 examples is a much larger update than the earlier attention-only/other configuration at the same nominal LR, so 'same LR 1e-4' does not mean same dose; the gate collapse and loop decline could both be simple over-fitting/instability of this configuration. No lower-LR loop is run in the final round (only the gate was repeated at 2e-5), so the decline of the loop is never checked at a rate where the gate is also failing for style reasons. Cross-round comparisons (and the claim that earlier flat results were 'recipe' effects) cannot be drawn.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Gate-failure attribution to reference style is asserted, not tested; competing explanation is a harmful training configuration that also applies to the loop
quote:
the failure
is not speciﬁc to the rate; we attribute it to the reference style but did not
isolate it.
explanation: Evidence offered: $-delimited spans rise from 60/1600 to 1577/1600 (98.6%) at 1e-4 and 1558/1600 (97.4%) at 2e-5. That shows style transfer, not that style causes a 29-32 point accuracy loss; $-delimited math is not itself wrong, and math-verify handles it. The accuracy drop could equally come from terse reference solutions that remove step-by-step reasoning (the paper notes in 4.5 that responses shorten by more than half), from lost \boxed formatting, or from over-fitting with all-linear LoRA. Only two rates (5x apart, both on the same 300 examples) were tried and the 2e-5 failure is nearly as large, which, if anything, suggests the problem is the content/format of the data rather than step size, but nothing separates these. Crucially, if the cause is the pipeline (masking, parsing, scoring of $-style answers by the exam verifier) rather than the data, then the loop's -4.1 may share it. A simple isolating check (re-score gate generations with a style-agnostic extractor, or train on the model's own unfiltered samples) is missing. The statement that the gate 'neither validates nor refutes the loop' is right, but then the headline interpretive weight placed on the loop falling 'probably costs a few points' is also unsupported.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: The final-round loop has no no-filter or equal-dose control, so the decline cannot be tied to the verifier; the research question is not answered by this round
quote:
The loop does not help and probably costs a few points;
we did not isolate the cause.
explanation: The paper's question is 'mathematics or the verifier?'. In the final round the only arms are verifier-filtered loop (298 examples) and train-on-gold (300 examples, a different data source). A decline of ~4 points is equally predicted by any fine-tuning of the model on its own samples with this configuration (e.g., loss of diversity, drift from the instruct model, sampled-at-temperature data), independent of the filter. The no-filter control used in earlier rounds is dropped here, so the decline is uninformative about verifier effects, and also does not distinguish 'self-training does not help' from 'this fine-tuning hurts'. Given the failed gate the authors are right to limit claims, but the abstract/5.1 sentence that the loop 'falls in each of three seeds' reads as evidence about the loop when the control that would make it so is absent.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Table 4 baseline is ambiguous: 'Untrained 49.2' is seed 1's draw, while seeds 2-3 are paired with 46.8 and 48.2
quote:
Change from
each run’s own untrained round 0 to round 1 in points (round-0 pass@1 is 49.2, 46.8,
48.2 at seeds 1–3, from sampling)
explanation: I checked the arithmetic. Per-seed changes -4.8, -3.2, -4.2 average -4.07, matching '-4.1'. Absolute round-1 pass@1 values implied are 49.2-4.8=44.4, 46.8-3.2=43.6, 48.2-4.2=44.0. So the three trained models are within 0.8 points of each other while the three 'untrained' measurements of the same model span 2.4 points; the between-seed spread of the change (SD 0.81) is mostly baseline sampling noise, not training-seed variation. A reader using the single 'Untrained 49.2 / 59.4' row would compute 44.4, 46.0, 45.0 for round 1, which is wrong for seeds 2 and 3. The gate (49.2 -> 17.0) and the 2e-5 rerun (49.2 -> 20.6) use seed 1's baseline only. The pooled untrained mean (48.07) is a better common baseline and should be tabulated, along with the untrained pass@2 per seed (only 59.4 is given). The sentence calls the baseline 'untrained', but the same untrained model measured three times gives 46.8-49.2, which also bounds how much of a 3-5 point change is sampling noise.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Table 4)

title: The t-interval over three seeds omits problem-sampling uncertainty shared by all seeds, so '[-6.1, -2.1]' is too narrow to carry the 'probably costs a few points' claim; interval claims use inconsistent bases
quote:
The mean pass@1
change over the three seeds is −4.1 (t interval [−6.1, −2.1]), and −4.5 for sample
accuracy ([−8.1, −1.0]).
explanation: Recomputed: pass@1 changes -4.8,-3.2,-4.2: mean -4.07, SD 0.81, SE 0.47, t(0.975,2)=4.303, half-width 2.01 -> [-6.08, -2.06] (matches). Sample accuracy -2.9,-5.3,-5.4: mean -4.53, SD 1.42, SE 0.82, half-width 3.52 -> [-8.05, -1.02] (matches). The arithmetic is right, but the intervals are conditional on the single set of 500 exam problems and a single selection pool of 300: they capture only seed-to-seed variation (including baseline sampling noise), whereas the per-seed bootstrap intervals (half-widths ~4.0-4.2 points, about twice the t half-width) capture problem-sampling error, which is common to all three seeds and not averaged down. The footnote in Table 4 says bootstrap intervals 'omit training-seed variance' while the t-interval omits problem variance; neither is a full interval and they are not combined (e.g. by resampling problems and averaging across seeds). With n=3 the t interval is also very unstable (t=4.3; SD from three points). Further, 'loses pass@1 in all three seeds' is based on point estimates, with the seed-2 interval [-6.8, +0.6] containing zero (and pass@2 seed 1 [-6.8,+0.6], sample-acc seed 1 [-5.8, 0.0] touching zero), so the 'loss' is a mixture of significant and non-significant results. The conclusion that a loss exists is plausible but the strength/precision is overstated.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Table 4)

title: 'Detectable effect about 6 points' is derived from single-run bootstrap half-width and mixes single-run and three-seed inference
quote:
The detectable eﬀect is about 6 points of pass@1
(2.8h/1.96), against about 10 before.
explanation: Check: per-seed pass@1 half-widths are 4.2, 3.8, 4.1; 2.8*4.1/1.96 = 5.9, so '6' is arithmetically consistent for a single run. But (i) it is the minimum detectable effect for one run and one seed (80% power at alpha 0.05), not for the three-seed mean the paper actually draws conclusions from; (ii) the half-width excludes training-seed variance (the abstract admits 'so likely more'), so the quoted 6 is a lower bound that is nevertheless used to say 'gains below about 6 could have been missed' without an upper estimate; (iii) the observed effects (-4.2 to -4.8) are below the nominal detectable 6, yet two of three single-run intervals exclude zero, which is consistent only because the observed effects are estimated at about 50-60% power; the text should not say effects <6 'could not be detected' and also draw detection conclusions from -4. The 10 vs 6 comparison also mixes 150 vs 500 exam problems and k=4/8 vs k=2, so 'against about 10 before' is not a like-for-like improvement. Low-severity but affects the interpretation of the null statement in the abstract and conclusions.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: 'Two rounds' vs a single change from round 0 to round 1; the second round is never reported
quote:
It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds; the loop has three
seeds, the gate one.
explanation: Table 4 and the text report only 'Change from each run's own untrained round 0 to round 1'. The design says two rounds, yet no round-2 numbers appear for either the loop or the gate, and the 298 kept examples appear to be only the round-1 training set. Either 'two rounds' means rounds 0 and 1 (then it should be stated, and this is a one-round loop with restart from base, not an iterated loop), or round 2 was run and omitted, which would be an unreported outcome in a paper that otherwise insists on pre-set reading rules. The headline 'self-training' claim concerns multiple rounds, so the reader cannot tell whether the decline compounds, recovers or is flat. Also unclear is whether the $-span counts (1,600 generations = 800 problems x k=2) refer to round 1 only.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Cleanliness of the 300-problem MATH-train pool vs MATH-500 and the base model is not documented; selection procedure of the pool unspecified
quote:
a pool of 300 problems from the MATH training split, so that the exam is all 500
MATH-500 problems.
explanation: Moving the pool to the MATH train split removes the earlier selection==eval circularity (a real improvement). However: (a) MATH-500 is itself a subset of the original MATH test split, so disjointness from MATH-train holds by construction only if the paper's pool excludes problems that appear in MATH-500 and near-duplicates; no dedup/overlap check is described (MATH has known near-duplicate problems across splits). (b) How the 300 were chosen (random, seed, difficulty/level stratification, subject mix) is not stated, though the pool composition determines the 298 kept examples, the gold-arm training data and the per-seed results (is the same pool used across all three seeds?). (c) Qwen2.5-Instruct was almost certainly trained on MATH-train problems and solutions, so 'train on gold' reference solutions may be seen data and the model's own samples on this pool are probably higher-accuracy than on unseen problems; this affects both the gate and the loop dose. The Limitations only mention 'possible test-set contamination' in a clause. For the 'matched' reading, the pool difficulty (selection acc ~50% -> 298 of 600 samples kept) should also be stated.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Injected-bias arithmetic and denominators are unclear: '70 of 500' exam problems vs a 300-problem selection pool, and '263 vs 298' kept
quote:
every \boxed answer is rejected when
the gold contains \frac (70 of 500 problems; 263 examples kept instead of 298).
explanation: The verifier bias is applied at selection time, and selection uses the 300-problem MATH-train pool, but the affected count is given as 70 of 500 (the exam size). It is unclear whether 70/500 (14%) is the exam fraction (used for the boxed-share split) while a different, unstated number of the 300 pool problems is affected. The kept examples fell by 35 (298 -> 263, -11.7%); if 14% of the 300 problems (~42) were affected and the model boxes ~90% of correct answers (Table values 90.2-95.0%), expected removal is roughly 42 x 2 x ~0.5 x 0.9 ~ 38, near 35, but if the affected fraction in the pool is 70/300 (23%) the expected drop would be ~60. The reader cannot reconstruct the dose. Because the hash arm is '30%' while the visible rule affects only 14% (exam) of problems, the two controls also differ in dose by roughly 2x, and the number kept in the hash arm is not given, so the two positive controls are not comparable. The rule also removes boxed training examples from just ~12% of the training set, which is a weak push relative to the generic 3-5 point fall in boxed share the unbiased runs already show.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Injected-bias result: share difference moves in the wrong direction and pass@1 falls 7.0 points, yet text says 'neither control shows an effect'
quote:
pass@1 falls 7.0 points ([−11.2, −3.0]).
The model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised, but neither control
shows an eﬀect, so neither validates the audit; we report no rt for them.
explanation: Numbers: affected-problem boxed share 95.0% (unchanged) vs others 90.2->87.4 (-2.8), difference +2.8 [-2.8, +8.3], compared with -3.7, -2.7, -5.5 in the unbiased seeds (mean -3.97). Penalising boxing on affected problems should make their share fall relative to the others (negative difference), but the observed difference is +2.8, about 6.8 points the opposite way from the prediction and from the unbiased mean, with a CI of +/-5.5 that is compatible with both zero and with the unbiased values. So the control is uninformative rather than showing 'no selective avoidance'; the sentence 'the model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised' is an absence-of-evidence statement presented as a finding, and the abstract's 'show no selective avoidance' compounds it. Separately, pass@1 falls 7.0 points with an interval excluding zero, versus -3.2 to -4.8 in unbiased seeds. The paper does not discuss this: 'neither control shows an effect' is only true for boxed share; if a rejected-\boxed selection (35 fewer, partly unboxed-only examples) lowers accuracy by ~2-4 points more than the unbiased loop, that is an effect, and exactly the sort of damage the audit should relate to. With one seed and unbiased SD 0.8 (prediction interval from the three unbiased seeds about [-8.1, -0.1]) the 7.0 is in the tail but not outside, so the comparison is inconclusive, which the text should say. The hash-arm pass@1 is not reported at all.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Bias controls described as 'positive controls for the audit' yet no r_t is computed, so they cannot function as such; and the hash control is by design incapable of showing an effect
quote:
As positive controls for the audit we reran the loop once each
(seed 1, 10−4) with a selection veriﬁer that rejects \boxed answers (exam veriﬁer
clean).
explanation: A positive control for an r_t audit must show that r_t (or its change) responds when selective avoidance is induced. The paper reports the boxed-share split rather than r_t ('we report no rt for them'), so what is tested is a different statistic from what the audit measures, and the conclusion in Sections 5/7 ('the audit has no positive control') rests on it. The authors acknowledge the hash arm 'could not elicit selective avoidance' by construction, so it is not a control at all and should not be counted as one of 'two injected-bias controls' in the abstract and conclusion ('two ... controls that showed no selective avoidance'). The visible-rule arm is one seed, with 35 fewer examples, so it is weak as well. Using n=1 seed for each while the loop itself varies by about +/-0.8 (seed spread) and bootstrap CIs +/-5 is also inadequate for detecting a 3-point differential. The stated outcome ('has little power') is consistent with this, but then calling them 'controls that showed no selective avoidance' overstates what was learned.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Final-round scoring uses a different verifier/normalisation than earlier rounds, yet it is compared and pooled narratively with them
quote:
Scores before the ﬁnal
round use the veriﬁer with the defect.
explanation: The abstract and Sec. 6 state earlier scores use the verifier with the gold-storage defect (rejecting 15.5-18.3% of correct answers), while the final round has 'normalised gold answers'. Hence round-0 accuracy for the final round (49.2 on all 500 MATH-500) is not on the same scale as earlier numbers (e.g. 50.0 in Design P), and the 'about 10 vs 6' detectable effects, the 'pass@1 falls 3.2-4.8' and earlier null results are not comparable measurements. In 5.1 the sentence 'No run raises pass@1 or pass@k with an interval excluding zero, at any rate; in the 500-problem final round pass@1 falls ...' lumps them as one body of evidence. In addition, since the pre-final runs had a defect that was kept constant, the final round also does not show whether the earlier null was driven by it (the paper acknowledges no dose control for the defect). The comparison should be flagged wherever final-round and earlier numbers appear together, and the pre-set reading rule (one-sided) is not applied to the final round, which shows a significant decline.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Headline research question is not answered by the evidence, and the title/abstract framing outruns what the study can say
quote: We ask: after several GVT rounds, is the model better at mathematics, or
explanation: The paper poses a two-branch question (better at mathematics vs. only learned what the verifier accepts). Sections 4-7 concede that neither branch can be answered: the first is a null for one recipe whose positive gate fails (training on reference solutions drops pass@1 by 32 points), and the second is 'untested' because the pre-set rule cannot fire when accuracy does not rise and the audit has no positive control. The title ('No Detectable Gain from Verifier-Filtered Self-Training of a 1.5B Model') and the opening sentences of the abstract and introduction nevertheless frame this as a study of self-training in general and of the verifier-vs-mathematics question. The question also presupposes a rising score to interpret, and the paper never observes one; what it observes is a decline. The honest qualifiers are present, but they are buried behind a title and framing that a reader would take as a statement about verifier-filtered self-training, when a failed positive control means the experiments cannot distinguish 'self-training does not help' from 'this training pipeline cannot improve this model at all'. The authors deserve credit for the candour; the issue is the mismatch between headline and warranted scope.
