title: The verifier 'bias' studied is largely a defect of the authors' own pipeline, yet is presented as a property of rule-based verifiers
quote: it rejects some correct answers written in forms it does not parse (Section 3.2).
explanation: The Introduction motivates the study by saying the rule-based verifier rejects correct answers. Section 3.2 shows the dominant rejection (15.5-18.3% of V'-accepted generations, and the unparseable-gold 10.2% of MATH-500 problems) comes from the pipeline storing gold answers without a delimiter, so that math-verify's LaTeX extraction is not applied; eight of ten false negatives in the format probe pass when only the boxed answer is verified. Wrapping the gold in $...$ or \boxed{} is the documented way to call math-verify, so this is an integration bug, not an intrinsic bias of rule-based verifiers. Only the \dfrac/\tfrac rejection is a genuine parser limitation, and the paper itself shows it touches 0-4 training examples. Consequently the narrative linking the study to TinyV, Egashira et al. and 'the verifier accepts what it accepts' overstates the relevance: most 'verifier bias' measured is harness error that a standard call would remove, and the paper's central audit (r_t) is about that bug. The related-work comparisons (e.g., recall of 0.95 for math-verify in [6], 86% average) suggest the properly configured verifier is considerably better than the one used here.

title: The audit measures false rejects, which by the paper's own account cannot create pressure to adapt in SFT, so it does not address the stated question
quote: used form of the loop, oﬄine rejection-sampling SFT, where a false reject only
explanation: The introduction itself says that in offline SFT 'a false reject only removes a training example', and Section 5.3 concludes 'Under SFT the pressure to adapt is therefore weak' (2-12 relevant training examples per round). Yet the research question is whether the model learns to write what the verifier accepts, and the audit is built on false-reject rates only. In rejection-sampling SFT, learning verifier-specific behaviour would show up chiefly through false accepts (wrong or unfaithful reasoning that ends in an accepted string), which the paper explicitly does not measure ('gives no false-positive rate'). Related Work also reports that Egashira et al. find systematic false negatives behave like random noise, which predicts no adaptation signal for a problem-bound defect like the one studied; the paper does not connect this prediction to its audit. The audit was therefore ill-matched to the question by construction, and its null/uninformative result says little about the 'second branch' it is supposed to probe. Carrying a per-step false-negative tracker from RLVR (where a false reject is a zero reward) into SFT (where it is a dropped example) changes what the quantity means.

title: The 'cheapest and most widely used form of the loop' is not what was implemented; the null may reflect a defective training recipe
quote: This paper studies the question in the cheapest and most widely
explanation: The paper claims to study the standard offline rejection-sampling SFT loop (STaR, ReST, ReST-EM, RFT) and that the result concerns 'this recipe'. But Section 3.4 and 4.6 reveal the main-run recipe deviates from those methods in ways that plausibly depress accuracy irrespective of the verifier: loss over the prompt as well as the completion, LoRA on q_proj/v_proj only, a 512-token training limit that cuts the final answer and EOS from 24-26% of kept examples (and 62.4% in no-filter), and fp16 on a T4. The positive gate, training on reference solutions, drops pass@1 by 32 points even with the corrected recipe, which signals the pipeline degrades a strong instruct model on any SFT data. The 'most widely used' characterisation is also unsupported by a citation. Because the one measure of whether the pipeline can help fails, the finding that 'verifier-filtered self-training' yields no gain is not separable from implementation. The authors state a recipe-only reading, which is appropriate, but the Introduction and Contributions still present it as the canonical cheapest GVT loop.

title: Contribution list credits an audit that the paper elsewhere calls not new and uninformative
quote: – A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect, carried over
explanation: The Contributions list presents the per-round false-reject audit as the second contribution. The Related Work then states that this measurement 'is not new: it is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV, applied to offline SFT' and that the authors 'do not claim the combination of a measured verifier bias and a patched control as a contribution'. The same bullet concedes the audit 'is uninformative about adaptation', and the injected-bias controls fail to validate it. Section 5.3 then relabels it 'a proposed audit' for future studies 'not as tested methods'. What remains as a contribution is the porting of an existing measurement to SFT, with no positive control and an effect that tracks \boxed share. The contribution is therefore an untested protocol, and calling it a contribution (and a headline element of the abstract) is stronger than the evidence supports; the contributions list should say so rather than listing it alongside the null result and the decomposition.

title: Introduction asserts the pooled decline 'does not reproduce under isolation' although Section 4.1 and 5.1 say the designs cannot be compared
quote: the solutions the model does ﬁnish. A sharp decline in a pooled design does not
explanation: The sentence continues 'reproduce under isolation (Section 4.1)', and the Conclusion repeats 'The pooled design's decline does not reproduce under isolation.' But Section 4.1 states the pooled design 'cannot be read causally' and that 'No run separates these explanations', and Section 5.1 says 'we cannot say whether pooling, selection-set scoring or dose produced it'. The pooled design differs from the isolated runs in dataset mix, one adapter over both pools, selection==evaluation, ~4.5x more training examples per round (3,962 vs 872), and also uses both model sizes. A non-reproduction across arms that differ in four or more factors is not a replication failure of any one of them. Moreover isolated runs at higher learning rates (5e-4: pass@1 down 4-11 points; Run C at 1e-5: -12.7; train-on-gold: -18 to -21) show substantial declines, so 'does not reproduce' is too absolute. The headline phrasing should be 'is not matched by the dose-lower isolated runs at 1e-5', not a statement of non-reproduction.

title: Abstract and Introduction present the cap-conditional 'finished accuracy' decline as a finding, but the decomposition attributes most of the decline to cap share in some runs
quote: ﬁnished-accuracy part and a cap-share part: at the highest rate, ﬁnished
explanation: Contribution 3 and the Introduction say that 'what appears, most clearly at the highest rate, is lower accuracy on the solutions the model does finish' and report a 5.5-10.6 point loss in finished accuracy. Section 4.5 reports that the three-part decomposition attributes 52-72% of the decline to cap share at seed 2 (and 12-30% at seed 1), and Table 1 shows the seed-2 5e-4 cap-hit share at 51.2% vs a round-0 level of ~43%. So at seed 2 the decline is mostly 'fewer solutions finish', not 'finished solutions are less accurate'. The matched finished-accuracy measure also conditions on which problems finish after training (post-treatment selection), which the paper admits makes it only descriptive; one of the six runs in the 5.5-10.6 range has an interval reaching +0.1, and the range pools A/B pairs, no-filter arms and different seeds that the paper elsewhere calls near-replicates. Calling this a contribution with a point range and 'cap-hit share rises only at that rate' is therefore stronger than the post hoc, descriptive evidence. Notably the Related Work credits Xu et al. [16] for the finished/terminated separation, so novelty is also limited.

title: Claim that the final-round loop 'falls' in each seed is stated more firmly in the abstract than the intervals support
quote: recipe, pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds (mean −4.1).
explanation: The abstract reports a pass@1 fall of 3.2-4.8 points in every seed. Table 4 shows that for seed 2 the pass@1 interval is [-6.8, +0.6] (includes zero), and the intervals omit training-seed variance and are based on a single sampled draw per problem at k=2; round-0 pass@1 itself varies 46.8-49.2 across seeds purely from sampling. Section 4.6 more cautiously says the loop 'probably costs a few points' and that 'we did not isolate the cause'. The three-seed t-interval [-6.1, -2.1] rests on n=3 and on seeds that share the same exam problems, and the whole final round is one of the analyses the Introduction lists as post hoc. The paper otherwise argues that the design can detect only ~6 points of pass@1 in this round, so a 4-point effect is below its stated resolution; reporting it as a consistent decline in the abstract is in tension with that. The abstract should carry the qualifier that the effect is below the stated detectable size and that pass@1 intervals include zero in one seed.

title: Pre-set rule and 'fixed in advance' measures are given weight although virtually every operative choice is post hoc and the rule was unable to fire
quote: (Section 4.6) were all added after seeing earlier runs; all are post hoc.
explanation: The Introduction invokes four measures 'fixed in advance' and a pre-set reading rule, then lists what was post hoc: the higher learning rates, controls, round count and k at those rates, sample accuracy as the primary measure, termination measures, the re-scoring for the second verifier defect, and the entire final 500-problem round. This leaves almost nothing confirmatory: the null at 1e-5 (which the paper says 'changed the outputs little') is the only pre-set arm, and its pre-set measure pass@1 has the lowest power (about 10 points). The rule was also one-sided, as the authors admit, so it could never have supported the 'verifier-style' branch. Nothing documents that the measures were truly fixed in advance (no preregistration or timestamped plan is cited). Because the pre-set framing is used to lend discipline to the 'no gain' claim, and the remaining analyses were chosen after seeing results, no multiplicity correction is applied across roughly twenty runs, and the headline 'no interval excludes zero' is a count of failed rejections under low power. The paper discloses all this, which is commendable, but the abstract's categorical 'No pass@1 or pass@k gain has a problem-level bootstrap interval excluding zero' sits on a design that was iterated until the end; the claim should be marked as exploratory rather than a test of the pre-set rule.

title: Related-work comparison between RLVR on base/Math models and SFT on an instruct model is not like-for-like and some characterisations are loose
quote: which our SFT loop does not; of Wang et al.’s 37.6 points only 8.6 lie beyond
explanation: The Introduction and Related Work use Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and base-model zero-RL results as the motivating benchmark of 'large gains at this scale', then contrast them with the null from an instruction-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B (Limitations: 'all instruction-tuned (no base model)'). Those gains are largely available because base/Math models have format and elicitation headroom (the paper itself notes only 8.6 of 37.6 points exceed format correction, and cites Shao et al. that rewards can be spurious and effects vary by model family), whereas an instruct model with a boxed-answer prompt starts near 49% on MATH-500 with little format headroom. The paper therefore sets up an expectation that the study's design cannot test, and the contrast 'which our SFT loop does not' compares RL with SFT, different base checkpoints, and different training algorithms in one step. Similarly, Related Work says Kim et al. [8] show a teacher-conditioned self-distillation shortens responses and cuts accuracy 'as our train-on-gold control does', but train-on-gold here is plain SFT on reference solutions, and Section 4.6 admits the cause is 'attributed to the reference style but not isolated', so the analogy is asserted rather than supported.

title: 'At any learning rate we tried' overstates the coverage of the learning-rate sweep, whose arms change several factors at once
quote: – For a 1.5B model, LoRA SFT and one rule-based veriﬁer, no gain is de-
explanation: The first contribution says no gain is detectable 'at any learning rate we tried', and the abstract says 'at four learning rates'. But Section 3.4 states 1e-5 was a default 'not tuned', and Section 4.4 says the 1e-4/2e-4/5e-4 runs differ from the 1e-5 runs in k (4 vs 8), rounds (3 vs 5), pool size and even the pass@k metric, so 'only 10^-4 to 5x10^-4 isolates the rate'. The grid is thus coarse (Limitations: 'coarse'), confounded, has 1-3 seeds per rate, and 5e-4 ran with only two seeds; the best-performing rate in the final round was a different, un-swept recipe. Every arm moves in the same direction (declines), including the gate at 2e-5 and 1e-4, suggesting the failure is not specific to rate, which undercuts reading the sweep as coverage of the learning-rate dimension. The claim should be that no gain appeared in the sampled configurations, not that learning rate has been covered.

title: Prose and Table 2 disagree on the seed-1 patch difference at 1e-5, and the reconciliation note is ambiguous
quote: A is −0.7 [−3.3, +2.0] points of pass@1 at seed 0 and +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] at
explanation: Table 2 gives pass@1 changes at 1e-5 of A,0 = −2.7, B,0 = −3.3, A,1 = −3.3, B,1 = −4.0. The B-minus-A differences are therefore −0.6 (seed 0, i.e. −0.67 = one problem) and −0.7 (seed 1). The text reports −0.7 at seed 0 and +0.0 at seed 1 'recomputed from the saved generations'. The parenthetical says Table 2 'lists values from the run logs that differ by one problem, giving −0.7', without saying which seed this applies to. Reading the table, it is seed 1 (−0.7 versus recomputed +0.0), not seed 0 (−0.6, which matches −0.7 up to rounding). The headline table in the paper therefore carries a number the authors themselves say is wrong, in the very comparison used to conclude the patch has no effect. The Table 2 caption reports only a pass@8 discrepancy (58.0 vs 58.7) for B, seed 1 and does not mention that the pass@1 value for this run is also affected. The direction of the conclusion is unchanged (both are about zero), but the paper should either correct Table 2 or state per seed and metric which values were replaced. It would also help to keep one scoring source for all numbers; at present Table 1, Table 2 and the prose mix log-based and re-scored values.
source_section: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: Design P explanations: the selection==eval confound cannot produce a decline, and the 4.5x-dose explanation is hard to square with the 5e-4 runs
quote: both datasets’ pools; it scores on the problems it selects from; and it trains on
explanation: Section 4.1 lists three confounds (shared adapter over two datasets, scoring on the problems it selects from, about 4.5x more training examples) and concludes the design 'cannot be read causally' and that 'no run separates these explanations'. I checked this against the paper's own numbers. (i) Selection==eval can only bias accuracy upward: training on the model's own verified-correct solutions to the very problems it is scored on should inflate, not deflate, exam accuracy. It therefore cannot be an explanation of a fall from 50.0% to 18.6% pass@1; it makes the collapse more surprising, not less interpretable. (ii) The dose explanation is quantitatively doubtful. Each round's model is a single adapter trained on the previous pool, with optimizer steps equal to half the pool (Section 3.4). Design P at 1e-5 with 3,962 examples is about 1,980 steps x 1e-5, roughly 0.02 in step-times-rate units at most (before linear decay). Design I at 5e-4 with about 390-440 examples is about 200 steps x 5e-4, roughly 0.1, about five times larger, yet it loses only 4-11 pass@1 points (Table 2), and no-filter at 3.6x the steps (about 700 steps) loses a similar amount (Table 3). Step-times-rate is a crude proxy, but nothing in the paper's own evidence shows a dose-response steep enough for a 4.5x pool at 1e-5 to cause a 31-point collapse. This leaves the dataset mixing (one adapter on GSM8K plus MATH data, with a much larger and easier GSM8K share of accepted examples) as the least-tested candidate. Section 4.4's own statement that no-filter at 3-4x the steps does not decline more than Run A cuts against the dose reading, while the same section uses dose to dismiss the no-filter comparison. The paper should state which of the three explanations the existing data disfavour instead of treating them as equally open, and note that the intro's 'does not reproduce under isolation' is itself a causal-sounding framing the section says it cannot support.

title: The 'replicate' reading of same-seed A/B and the +5.3 to −7.3 'flip' rest on single-sample pass@1; sample accuracy shows a much smaller flip
quote: is +5.3 at seed 1 and −7.3 [−14.0, −0.7] at seed 2, a sign ﬂip from pools that
explanation: The paper uses the B-minus-A sign flip in round-2 pass@1 (+5.3, −7.3) as the central evidence of large training-trajectory noise (Section 3.4, 4.4), and so for treating same-seed A/B as 'closer to two replicates than four' and for calling reported intervals optimistic. I recomputed from Table 2 at 5e-4. B minus A in pass@1: seed 1 = −4.7 − (−10.0) = +5.3; seed 2 = −11.3 − (−4.0) = −7.3 (correct). But pass@1 uses one draw per problem (Section 3.4), so for p around 0.3 and n = 150 the sampling SD of a single pass@1 is about 3.7 points and the SD of a difference of two independent runs about 5.2 points. A 5-7 point gap is therefore only about 1-1.4 SD of pure resampling noise and does not by itself reveal trajectory instability. On the paper's own preferred, lower-variance measure (sample accuracy over four draws), B minus A is −6.7 − (−8.3) = +1.6 at seed 1 and −9.2 − (−4.7) = −4.5 at seed 2: a smaller flip. For pass@4 it is +5.3 and −4.6. Further problems with the replicate reading: (a) the seed-2 B-minus-A interval [−14.0, −0.7] excludes zero, which the text dismisses as 'trajectory noise' without showing that noise (rather than the patch) is the cause, since no true replicate (same seed, same verifier, differently shuffled data) exists; (b) same-seed pairs share exam partition and selection set, whereas Section 3.4's 'one same-configuration replicate pair' (3.2 points apart) is not identified and cannot be matched to any pair in Tables 1-2; the three-seed 1e-4 runs differ by 5 points in round-2 sample accuracy (32.2, 27.2, 27.5) but those also differ in exam partition, so training noise and partition noise are not separated; (c) the one-seed-pair evidence is then used to inflate all detectable-effect numbers ('probably larger') with no estimate of the actual variance. A correct replicate estimate needs at least two runs that differ only in training randomness, or a variance decomposition across seeds for a measure like sample accuracy.

title: 'No detectable gain' is stated as a per-interval null, but the pooled sign pattern points to a decline that the text declines to name
quote: We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
explanation: The paper makes no multiplicity correction and says it rests conclusions on 'patterns across runs and seeds', but does not actually analyse the pattern. From Table 2 (MATH-500 A/B runs, excluding C and controls): sample-accuracy changes are all negative in 9 of 9 runs at 1e-5, 1e-4 and 2e-4 (−2.4, −1.5, −3.2, −1.2, −1.5, −3.7, −1.0, −3.5, −3.8; mean about −2.4), and pass@1 changes are negative in 12 of 13 A/B runs (only A,1 at 1e-4 is +0.7), all 13 at or below +0.7. A one-sided sign test treating runs as independent gives p of about 0.002 (12 of 13) and 0.002 (9 of 9), though runs share the same 150 problems within a seed, so the real evidence is weaker; the correct analysis is a pooled mixed model over seeds and problems, which the paper does not report. The 'no gain' claim itself is safe against multiplicity (no interval is positive, so there is no false-positive to correct), but the descriptive claims that are quoted use post hoc subsets ('only for B at seed 0', 'five of six runs', 'the six include two same-seed pairs') that are exactly where multiplicity matters. The text also hedges the declines ('possible small decline, not an established one') while treating no-gain as established, which is an asymmetric standard. Since the Abstract and Section 5.1 state the null as 'not detectably' better, the paper should either report the pooled estimate and interval (which likely excludes zero for sample accuracy), or explain why a consistent sign pattern is not informative. Also, the observed upper limits (up to +8 for pass@1, +2.2 for sample accuracy) are much tighter than the 10-point 'detectable effect', so the statement 'a gain of the size the design could detect' undersells what the data exclude for sample accuracy and oversells what they exclude for pass@1.

title: Rate dependence is not shown: 1e-5 and 1e-4 give the same decline, which undercuts the 'adapter did little at 1e-5' rationale
quote: length and cap-hit share, barely change, which is weak evidence that the adapter
explanation: Section 4.4 motivates the higher-rate runs by 'Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little' and Section 4.2 supports that with unchanged length and cap-hit share. But Table 2 shows the mean sample-accuracy change is about −2.1 at 1e-5 (A/B, four runs: −2.4, −1.5, −3.2, −1.2) and about −2.1 at 1e-4 (−1.5, −3.7, −1.0), i.e. a tenfold increase in rate changes nothing, whereas 5e-4 gives −8.3 and −4.7 and 2e-4 gives −3.5 and −3.8. The decline therefore does not scale with rate over 1e-5 to 1e-4, and at seed 2 it is 'almost flat' (3.7, 3.8, 4.7) over 1e-4 to 5e-4. The only monotone trace is seed 1 (1.5, 3.5, 8.3) from a single partition. The text's 'may grow with the rate' is thus based on one seed, while the other seed shows a flat response, and the 1e-5 runs (which differ in k, rounds and metric) are not on this axis anyway. If the 1e-5 adapter did little, a decline of similar size at 1e-4 is difficult to attribute to the adapter at all; alternatively the 1e-5 adapter did change behaviour (Run C falls 12.7 points at the same rate with about 2x steps), so 'changed the outputs little' is not a safe premise. In either case, causal statements like 'decline may grow with the rate' and, in the Introduction, 'most clearly at the highest rate' need to be restricted to what two seeds at 5e-4 show, and the constant floor of about −2 at low rate (possibly a measurement or round-0 sampling artefact, since round-0 pass@1 itself varies from 29.3 to 33.3 across seeds) should be discussed.

title: Cap-share decomposition is not reproducible from the main text, and a direct computation gives a seed-2 share far above the reported 52-72%
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
explanation: Table 1 gives the ingredients for a simple decomposition: sample accuracy = f x a, with f the finished share (1 minus the cap-hit share) and a the finished accuracy. For A at 5e-4, seed 1: round-0 cap share 43.2% (f0 = 0.568), round-2 46.2% (f2 = 0.538), sample accuracy 33.7 to 25.3. Then a0 = 59.3% and the cap-share term (Δf x a0) = −3.0 x 0.593 = −1.8 points, about 21% of the −8.4 decline, inside the stated 12-30%. For seed 2: cap share 43.0% to 51.2% (Δf = −8.2 points), sample accuracy 30.8 to 26.2, a0 = 54.0%, so the cap-share term is −8.2 x 0.54 = −4.4 points, about 96% of the −4.6 decline, versus the reported 52-72%. The reported matched finished accuracy for A,2 is −5.5 points, which would add a further −3 points for a total near −7.5, larger than the actual −4.7, so the three parts as described cannot be additive without a large positive cross term. The text never says how the 'three-part decomposition' and 'matched' measures treat problem mix, so these figures cannot be checked. The numbers also vary widely by run (12-30%, −2%, 5%, 52-72%), and for seed 2 the cap share, not finished accuracy, carries the majority of the decline, which conflicts with the Introduction and contribution bullet ('What appears, most clearly at the highest rate, is lower accuracy on the solutions the model does finish') and with the statement that finished accuracy 'carries the whole change' at lower rates (those declines are of the same size at seed 2: 3.7 to 3.8). The mechanism is thus seed-dependent, and magnitudes of declines alone (flat across rates at seed 2) hide different mechanisms. Please define the decomposition in the main text and reconcile it with Table 1.

title: Pool-size and 'differ by' figures use inconsistent units and values across sections and tables
quote: \dfrac appears in 0.50–0.73% of generations, so the kept pools diﬀer by 3–4
explanation: The A-versus-B pool difference is given as 0–4 examples in Section 3.2, 3–4 examples in Section 4.3 and 0–3 examples in Section 4.4; these ranges are not nested sensibly (3-4 vs 0-3) and do not say which learning rate and k they apply to. Separately, Table 3 reports kept pools of 440 to 326 and 424 to 350 (examples; up to 4 per problem), while Table 1's added/lost counts are problems solved by at least one of 4 samples (22/33 and 26/36), and Section 3.4 states added minus lost equals 150 x Δpass@k. I checked this identity against Table 1 and it holds for all seven rows (e.g. 22 − 33 = −11 = 150 x (−7.3%)). But a reader comparing 'problems added/lost' of −11 with a pool contraction of 114 examples (440 to 326) may take them to describe the same quantity; the Table 3 caption does not state the unit, and does not state that round 0 to round 2 means the round-2 model uses the middle pool (392 or 386) rather than the endpoint figures in the column. The 'about 195 steps' (392/2 = 196, 386/2 = 193) is consistent, and the 4.5x pool ratio (3,962 vs 872) checks out. The unit and range inconsistencies are minor but affect how a reader judges the 'trajectory noise from near-identical pools' argument, which depends on exactly how identical the pools are.
source_section: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: No-filter versus filtered comparison is summarised through pass@4 only; other metrics show a mixed or reversed sign
quote: lower on pass@4 at both seeds (round-2 diﬀerences −2.0 and −5.3
explanation: The text says removing the filter 'is not better than keeping it beyond noise and is lower on pass@4 at both seeds'. From Table 2/3 at 5e-4: pass@4 no-filter minus A = −2.0 (seed 1) and −5.3 (seed 2), correct. But pass@1 no-filter minus A in round 2 is 27.3 − 23.3 = +4.0 at seed 1 and 22.7 − 27.3 = −4.6 at seed 2, and sample accuracy is −8.2 − (−8.3) = +0.1 at seed 1 and −10.2 − (−4.7) = −5.5 at seed 2. So the direction is consistent only for one of the three measures, and at seed 1 the sample accuracy (the paper's preferred measure) is identical for the two arms. Selecting the one metric with a consistent sign, among several available, is the same selection that the paper elsewhere warns about (post hoc metrics). Moreover, the no-filter arm uses 3.6x the optimizer steps (1,400 examples against 392 or 386), yet its decline is no larger than the filtered run at seed 1; that undermines the idea that a larger dose should be expected to produce more decline, which the paper uses in Section 4.1 to explain the Design P collapse. The sentence should report all three measures and conclude plainly that the comparison is uninformative, rather than leaning on the pass@4 sign.

title: Post hoc 'detectable effect' conflicts with the CI-based reading and with the 2.2-point bound; one-sided rule vs two-sided formula
quote: detected with 80% power at the 5% level only if it exceeded about 2.8 h/1.96:
explanation: The constant is right for a two-sided 5% test at 80% power: (1.96+0.84)*SE with SE=h/1.96. I checked it against Table 2: h of about 6.7 for pass@1 gives about 9.6, and h of about 4.2 in Section 4.6 gives about 6. Three things remain. (a) The paper's pre-set reading rule is one-sided (it fires only when pass@1 rises), and the claim under test is 'no gain'. A one-sided test would use 1.645+0.84, which is about 1.27h, or about 8.5 points rather than 10. So the headline 'about 10 points' is not tied to the paper's own decision rule. (b) After the data are in, a CI already says which gains are excluded. Every Delta-pass@1 interval in Table 2 has an upper limit of at most +8.0 (and the Gold/C rows are wider for other reasons). Reporting 'gains below about 10 points could have been missed' uses a pre-data power concept that is more pessimistic than the paper's own intervals, and it mixes two logics. Sections 3.4/5.1 then add a third figure, 'about 2.2 points' of sample accuracy, defined as the largest upper limit among observed intervals. That is a CI-exclusion statement, so it is the same kind of statement as (b), and it sits next to a 3.5-5.5 'detectable' figure for the same measure with no explanation of why one is a bound and the other is not. A reader cannot tell which number states what the experiment rules out. (c) The 150-problem exam (a 30% holdout of 500) is given no power rationale. It was fixed before any power computation, and the final round shows that 500 problems halve the detectable effect. The 'null' for Runs A-C is therefore weak by construction, and the abstract's 'about 10 points' headline should be stated as a consequence of that design choice.

title: Headline power uses single-draw pass@1 although a lower-variance estimator of the same quantity is available
quote: is the correctness of the ﬁrst of the k samples (one draw per problem, so it
explanation: pass@1 is defined from only the first of k=8 (or 4, or 2) samples, so each exam problem contributes one Bernoulli draw even though 3-7 further samples per problem were generated. The paper admits that sample accuracy 'estimates the same quantity from all k samples with less variance'. Its own numbers show the cost: detectable pass@1 is about 10 points and sample accuracy is 3.5-5.5, so about 2x worse precision from discarding data. The abstract and Introduction nevertheless lead with pass@1 as the measure 'fixed in advance', and present '10 points' as how insensitive the design is. That figure is mostly an artefact of the estimator. For the same estimand the design is roughly twice as sensitive, and the paper then declines to treat the sample-accuracy figure as a power statement because the measure was chosen after the runs. The result is that the pre-set measure is the noisy one and the sensitive measure is demoted as post hoc, so neither gives a clean statement. A related point: pass@k is the raw 'at least one of k samples' indicator, and k differs across runs (8, 4, 2), so 'pass@k flat' in the pre-set rule is not a common quantity across the learning-rate arms. The first sample is also treated as exchangeable; the paper does not say how it was indexed (batch position, seed), so a position effect cannot be excluded.

title: No multiplicity correction and runs treated as independent evidence although they share exam partitions and round-0 draws
quote: We make no multiplicity correction, so we rest conclusions on patterns across
explanation: The paper replaces correction with 'patterns across runs and seeds', but the runs are not independent. A seed fixes the exam partition, the selection set and training randomness at once, and runs at the same seed share the partition. Table 1 shows identical round-0 numbers (33.3 pass@1, 33.7 sample accuracy at seed 1 for every learning rate), so the 1e-4, 2e-4 and 5e-4 rows at a seed share one round-0 draw and one exam. Run A and B at the same seed are, in the authors' own words, 'closer to two replicates than four'. The effective number of independent confirmations behind statements such as 'at 5x10^-4 every run declines' or 'the decline may grow with the rate' is therefore about two to three partitions, not 7-12 runs. Over the roughly 60 intervals in Table 2 (4 metrics x 15 rows), some 'excludes zero' results are expected by chance, and the paper selects a few of them for narrative (e.g. B at seed 0 at 1e-5, A/B at 5e-4). The uncorrected intervals favour the claimed declines more than they favour the 'no gain' null. In the other direction, that no gain interval excludes zero among about 30 pass@1/pass@k intervals is the expected outcome under a true null, which is not strong support for 'no gain' either. A family-wise or at least a pooled-by-partition analysis (a mixed model with exam partition and seed as random effects) would be the consistent standard for a paper that says it needs to be rigorous about uncontrolled variance.

title: The replicate pair used to show that intervals are too narrow is not identified, and seed variance is confounded with exam partition
quote: conﬁguration replicate pair we have ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart.
explanation: This sentence is the paper's only direct evidence of how much the bootstrap intervals understate uncertainty, and it carries the argument that the detectable effects 'are lower bounds, probably larger'. But the pair is not identified. Section 3.3 says a seed sets the exam partition, the selection set and the training randomness at once, and that repeating Run A at a second seed 'draws a different 150-problem exam set'. If the pair is A at seed 0 versus A at seed 1, the 3.2-point difference in levels is mostly exam-set difficulty (round-0 sample accuracies of 28.5-33.7 across partitions in Table 1 show how large that is). It is not training-seed variance. The paired quantity that matters is the change from round 0, and for A that is -2.4 vs -1.5, a difference of 0.9. If it is A versus B at the same seed, it is not a same-configuration pair. Either way a single pair gives no variance estimate (one difference, zero degrees of freedom for a standard deviation), and the sign flip of B-A (+5.3 to -7.3) comes from different partitions as well. Because the seed bundles three sources, the paper cannot say how much of the spread is training noise, and the quantitative claim 'probably larger' has no stated basis. Training-seed variance with a fixed partition (several adapters on the same data and exam) was not run, even though the paper cites Xu et al. [16] for exactly this failure.

title: r_t takes V' acceptance as ground truth but V' is unvalidated and only 'repairs' boxed predictions
quote: the saved generations with a veriﬁer V ′ that wraps the gold in \boxed{} when
explanation: The central quantity r_t (and the 'about one in six' in the abstract) is the share of V'-accepted generations that V rejects, so it reads as a false-reject rate of V only if V' accepts are truly correct. The probe of Section 3.2 audited V on other models' solutions and, as the paper itself says, inspected only rejections. No false-positive check of V' on the 1.5B model's generations is reported. The wrapped gold is compared by math-verify's symbolic equivalence inside \boxed{}, which can accept a wrong answer, e.g. a differently scoped expression, a set versus an element, or an equality form. Such acceptances would be counted as 'false rejects' by V. Second, V' is a repair only 'when the prediction contains' \boxed{}. For unboxed predictions V' equals V, so a correct unboxed answer rejected for the same bare-gold reason is rejected by both and leaves both numerator and denominator of r_t. The denominator therefore changes with the boxed share, which is what the discussion later observes (boxed share among correct answers 91 to 76%), and this makes r_t a moving mixture of two verifiers rather than a clean defect rate. The paper notes part of this in Section 5.3, but the 15.5-18.3% figure is used as the defect's size in the abstract, in Section 3.2, in the dose argument (440 to 542) and in the 0.73-0.85 ratio, without a measured V' error rate.

title: Independent false-negative probe (7.8%, upper limit 13.8%) does not reconcile with the 15.5-18.3% rejection used as the defect size
quote: malised comparison) the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128; Wilson interval
explanation: I recomputed the interval: 10/128 = 7.8%, and the Wilson 95% interval is about [4.3, 13.8], matching the text. That upper limit lies below the 15.5-18.3% reported in the next paragraphs for the share of V'-accepted generations rejected by V. The probe measures all rejection causes (the 10 false negatives include the defect plus any extraction failures), so its rate should be at least the defect's rate if both populations were alike. The paper explains neither the factor of about 2 nor why the probe should be representative. Plausible reasons are that Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct solves a different, easier, set of problems than the 1.5B model, that the defect is problem-bound (54-62 of 500 problems), or that V' also accepts some wrong answers. Each of these would mean the 7.8% cannot be carried to the loop's own generations, so the probe does not validate the number the paper headlines. Further weaknesses in the probe: the reference is a 'scripted normalised comparison' that is itself unvalidated, so errors correlated with the verifier (same normalisation tricks) would hide false negatives or create false ones; only 200 problems and one solution each are used; the '0% on GSM8K' figure has no n or interval (with n of about 100-200 an upper limit of 2-3% would still apply); and 'probably largely the gold-storage defect' is a guess from 'most are compound answers', not a test.

title: 'Bound to the problem' rests on a set of problems defined by the defect firing, so rejection rates of 94-98% are inflated
quote: problem, not to the answer: on the 54–62 problems where it ever ﬁres, it rejects
explanation: The 'affected' set is defined ex post as problems where V' accepted and V rejected at least once. Conditioning on at least one rejection guarantees every included problem has a rejection and removes any problem where the defect is present but the sampled correct answers happened to pass (or were all unboxed). Problems with one or two correct samples, a typical case here with k=4 and pass rates of 30-45%, are then rejected 100% by construction. The 94-98% figure, and the inference 'bound to the problem, not to the answer', are partly an artefact of this selection. The same set also feeds Table 5's 'affected, parseable' rows (87-98% rejection) and the argument that 'no answer form escapes it'. A fair estimate needs the affected set defined from the gold side (golds without delimiter whose parse in V fails under a boxed prediction) independent of the generations, or at least held-out generations. Note also that 29-34 of the 54-62 have gold V cannot parse at all, so for more than half the set the 100% rejection is by definition, and only the remaining 24-28 problems speak to whether the answer form matters. The 'in every round' wording also hides that these problems contribute 2-12 pool examples.

title: Denominators of the defect statistics are not aligned (pool 440→542 vs r_t over all 500 problems; 'a fifth to a quarter')
quote: a quarter (440 →542, +23%), against 0–4 examples for the \dfrac patch, and
explanation: The arithmetic 542/440 = 1.232 is right. But the paper presents it beside 'rejects 15.5–18.3% of the generations V′ accepts'. In the same run the share of V'-accepted pool examples that V rejects is (542-440)/542 = 18.8%, outside the stated 15.5-18.3% range and above the Table 5 value of 18.3% for seed 1. The two numbers cover different sets: the pool counts accepted solutions of the 350 selection problems of one seed (k=4 gives 1,400 generations), r_t counts all 500 problems (2,000 generations). The text never says which set each number is computed on, or which seed 440/542 refers to (Table 3 has 440 for seed 1 and 424 for seed 2; no 542-equivalent is given for seed 2). The phrase 'by about a fifth to a quarter' is also ambiguous between 18.8% of the V' pool and 23% of the V pool. The range 15.5-18.3% mixes round 0 and last-round values across runs, while the gold arm (18.0-21.5%) lies outside it. The dose argument in Section 5.3(iii) ('about a fifth to a quarter of the pool') depends on these figures. It is a small inconsistency in size, but it is a place where a careful reader could take away a different number than the data support.

title: About 10% of golds are unscorable and the cancellation assumption is left unchecked although V' makes the check possible
quote: 500 stored MATH-500 golds (10.2%); these problems always count as unsolved,
explanation: 51/500 = 10.2% is correct. Together with the 54-62 problems where the defect rejects 94-98% of correct answers (29-34 of which overlap with the unparseable golds), roughly 15% of MATH-500 problems are effectively unscorable under V, and about 11-18 of the 150 exam problems per partition. Three consequences are not followed through. (1) The effective exam size is about 130 problems, so the intervals and the 10-point detectable effect are computed on a denominator that includes problems that cannot change. (2) The unparseable and defect-affected problems are not random: they are the ones whose answers are fractions, expressions or sets. The training pool therefore can contain only simple-answer problems (integers, plain decimals), so the loop trains on a biased stratum while the exam score has a ceiling. This is a form of the 'directional bias' the paper studies, but it is treated only as an offset. (3) The paper says the offset cancels in within-run differences 'only if those problems would not otherwise change, which we did not check'. That check is cheap here: V' already exists and was used to re-score five runs. Reporting Delta-pass@1 and Delta-pass@k under V' (or excluding the unscorable set) would show whether the null on the pre-set measures survives. Instead only sample accuracy is re-scored, so the headline null on pass@1/pass@k remains under a verifier the paper itself describes as biased.

title: r_t (Table 5) is computed on all 500 problems, mixing problems the adapter was trained on with unseen exam problems
quote: set; generation runs on all 500 problems each round, but only the other 350 can
explanation: I checked the partition for leakage into the exam: the 150 exam problems are excluded from the pool, so the accuracy tables (computed on the exam only) are not contaminated by training on exam problems. That part is sound. The audit is not so protected. Table 5 is 'all 500 problems', that is, 350 selection problems plus 150 exam problems, and the round-t adapter was trained on solutions the loop accepted for the 350 selection problems at round t-1. A fall in r_t on those 350 problems can arise from memorising the specific accepted (V-passing, i.e. defect-avoiding) solutions it was trained on. The question the audit asks is whether the model generalises 'avoid the defect' to problems it has not been trained on. The two cannot be separated without reporting r_t on the exam set and the selection set separately. This weakens the adaptation reading in either direction (a fall may be memorisation; a flat r_t on unseen problems may hide it), and the 'affected problems' count of 54-62 and 24-28 combines both sets. The related fact that a seed also sets the partition means different seeds audit different mixes of seen and unseen problems. Splitting by exam/selection costs nothing since the saved generations exist.

title: The 512-token budget makes the exam partly a termination test, and training truncation teaches unfinished answers
quote: prompt length is cut in training and loses its ﬁnal answer and end-of-sequence
explanation: Three recipe choices combine here. First, evaluation uses T=0.8 with a 512-token cap and the checkpoint's repetition penalty of 1.1 (which penalises repeating digits and LaTeX tokens). The paper's own Table 1 shows that 43% of round-0 generations hit the cap, so the measured 'mathematics' is bounded by whether the model finishes within 512 tokens. Round-0 pass@1 is about 33% on the 150-problem exam but 49.2% in Section 4.6 with a 1,024 cap on 500 problems; the partition spread seen in Table 1 (28.5-33.7 sample accuracy) cannot account for 16 points, so the cap and decoding appear to cost much of the base model's ability. Second, because the training limit equals the generation cap and includes the prompt, 24-26% of the kept pool is cut in training and loses its final answer and end-of-sequence token, so the loop trains on a quarter of examples that are unfinished by construction, together with a loss over the prompt. Third, the paper's Section 4.5 says retraining without truncated examples 'leaves the deficit in place', so truncation is not the sole cause. But the practical result is that Runs A-C and the 1e-5 to 5e-4 arms test a recipe the authors later describe as having 'suspected causes' of non-improvement. The abstract and title ('Mathematics or the Verifier?', 'No Detectable Gain from Verifier-Filtered Self-Training of a 1.5B Model') generalise beyond that. The scope is stated honestly in places, but the earlier arms are 'defective by design' as tests of self-training, and only the 500-problem final round (k=2, two rounds, one LR) uses the corrected recipe.

title: Training procedure underspecified: effective batch size, pool composition and per-problem handling of samples, seeds, precision
quote: weight decay at the library defaults; batch size 2; one epoch; AdamW with linear
explanation: The method is described as reproducible but several parameters that determine the dose and its meaning are missing or left to defaults. (a) 'Batch size 2' is not identified as per-device, with or without gradient accumulation, or as effective; the step counts (195 for 392/386 examples, 436 for 872) fit effective batch 2 with no accumulation, which I checked: 392/2 = 196 and 386/2 = 193, so the paper's 'about 195' is consistent. With effective batch 2, learning rates up to 5e-4, no warmup, fp16 on a T4 and no mention of gradient clipping or loss scaling, the 5e-4 declines (and the train-on-gold collapse) could come from optimisation instability rather than from what the data teaches, and the grid over learning rate cannot be separated from step noise. (b) LoRA dropout and weight decay are 'at the library defaults' without values, for three libraries whose defaults changed across versions (transformers 5.0.0, TRL 1.10.0). (c) How accepted samples are handled per problem is not stated: whether the up-to-k correct samples of one problem are all kept, deduplicated or capped. The 872 examples from 350 problems (k=8) suggest several near-identical solutions of easy problems per problem, so the pool is weighted toward easy problems, which shapes what 'filtering' does. (d) Which random seeds control generation, partition and training are not separated, and round-0 samples appear to be reused across learning rates (identical round-0 values in Table 1). (e) The pooled design's LR, round count and 0.5B settings are left to a supplement. These choices are central to claims about dose and about the 'no-filter' and 'gold' controls.

title: '4.5x dose' compares a two-dataset pooled pool (3,962) with a single-dataset isolated pool (872), so it is not a like-for-like dose
quote: about 4.5× as many examples per round as the isolated MATH-500 run (3,962
explanation: The arithmetic is right (3,962/872 = 4.54). But the two pools differ in more than dose. The pooled design trains one adapter on both datasets with all 1,000 problems eligible, while the isolated MATH-500 run uses MATH only and only 350 selection problems. The 872 is also at k=8 on MATH-500, where the 1.5B accuracy is about a third, whereas the pooled pool includes GSM8K, with a much higher acceptance rate. Using the paper's own statement that Run C took about twice Run A's optimizer steps, the isolated MATH and GSM8K pools together would be roughly 2.6k examples, and scaled to 500 problems each about 3.7k, almost the pooled 3,962. So most of the 4.5x is the structural consequence of pooling two datasets (and of not holding out 150 problems), not a free 'dose' knob that the isolated design failed to match. This matters because the paper repeatedly says the collapse 'cannot be attributed to pooling' on the grounds of dose (Sections 4.1, 5.1, 5.3(iv)). Pooling and dose are inseparable in this contrast, and the statement that a dose-matched isolated run would test pooling needs a clearer account of what matched dose means (per adapter, per problem, or per dataset).

title: No training-pipeline sanity check or frozen/zero-effect control, despite citing it as the standard
quote: to the base model and trained on the kept solutions for one epoch. Round 0 is
explanation: Related Work presents Xu et al. [16] as the closest study, auditing self-improvement 'against a frozen control' and naming training-seed variance and a fixed token cap as failures that 'each invert a finding when uncontrolled'. The present design does not apply that standard to itself. There is no control that trains an adapter on a random or unfiltered subset at matched dose and step count (the no-filter control triples the steps), no adapter trained at zero or negligible effective learning rate to calibrate resampling noise, and a replicate pair that is not clearly a replicate (see the replicate-pair finding). The only positive control, training on reference solutions, drops pass@1 from 49.2 to 17.0 and from 49.2 to 20.6 at a rate five times smaller, with 300 examples and about 150 steps. A drop of that size from a few hundred gold solutions, at two learning rates, is at least as consistent with a defect in the training or formatting pipeline (EOS handling, chat template, truncation at 1,024, fp16 on a T4) as with 'the reference style', which the paper says it 'did not isolate'. Without a sanity check that the pipeline can fit a trivially learnable target without degrading generation, the conclusion that the 'null concerns this recipe' is weaker than the abstract suggests, since the recipe may not be a faithful implementation of self-training.
